https://www.politico.eu/feed/.lastBody:
POLITICO https://www.politico.eu European Politics, Policy, Government News Mon, 02 Nov 2026 20:57:05 +0000 en hourly 60 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.11 Les lobbies du tabac mettent le paquet à Bruxelles, alors que l’UE se penche sur le secteur https://www.politico.eu/article/le-lobby-du-tabac-met-le-paquet-a-bruxelles-alors-que-lue-se-penche-sur-le-secteur/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Mon, 02 Nov 2026 20:57:00 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro-free&p=9234872 Les députés européens ont eu quatre fois plus de réunions avec les lobbyistes du tabac et de la nicotine au cours des deux dernières années que lors de l’intégralité de la législature précédente, selon les données analysées par POLITICO.

Depuis leur entrée en fonction à l’été 2024, les parlementaires ont déclaré plus de 400 réunions, contre une centaine environ au cours de la législature 2019-2024, selon les données collectées par le Smoke Free Partnership, une coalition d’ONG, à partir du registre de transparence. Dans ce dernier, les eurodéputés sont tenus de déclarer leurs réunions et ces informations sont rendues publiques.

Par ailleurs, la plupart des rencontres organisées au cours de la législature actuelle ont eu lieu avec des élus de droite. Environ 75% d’entre elles concernent des membres du Parti populaire européen (dont font partie Les Républicains), des Conservateurs et réformistes européens (dont fait partie Fratelli d’Italia de Giorgia Meloni), et du groupe d’extrême droite des Patriotes pour l’Europe (dont fait partie le Rassemblement national).

Les réunions avec l’industrie du tabac et de la nicotine se sont multipliées au cours de cette législature, alors que l’Union européenne s’apprête à réformer plusieurs législations importantes relatives au tabac et à la nicotine. Elle a également proposé, toujours lors de cette législature, des mesures visant à lutter contre les maladies cardiaques et le cancer, des projets qui ont des répercussions sur ces filières.

Certains députés européens ont dénoncé l’accès aux parlementaires dont bénéficie l’industrie du tabac, alors que ceux-ci négocient des mesures visant à prévenir la dépendance et les maladies causées par les produits de ce secteur, notamment dans le cadre d’un rapport sur la stratégie de lutte contre les maladies cardiovasculaires et d’un plan de lutte contre le cancer.

“Je trouve scandaleux et choquant qu’il y ait davantage de réunions avec l’industrie du tabac qu’avec les ONG et les associations qui militent pour l’arrêt du tabac”, s’est insurgée Tilly Metz, eurodéputée membre des Verts.

“Quand on travaille sur des dossiers liés à la santé, c’est tout à fait incompatible de rencontrer régulièrement les représentants de l’industrie du tabac”, a-t-elle considéré, en référence à la Convention-cadre de l’Organisation mondiale de la santé (OMS) pour la lutte antitabac, qui stipule que les décideurs politiques ne devraient rencontrer les lobbyistes du tabac que lorsque cela est strictement nécessaire pour discuter de la réglementation du secteur.

L’industrie du tabac et les députés européens qui rencontrent régulièrement les représentants de ce secteur affirment n’avoir rien fait de mal.

Simon Trussler, responsable des affaires fiscales chez British American Tobacco, a objecté que, comme toute autre entreprise en Europe, celle-ci avait une expérience et des arguments légitimes à faire valoir, “car nous voyons ce qui se passe sur le terrain”.

Philip Morris International, le fabricant des cigarettes Marlboro, dont le nombre de réunions est le plus élevé parmi toutes les entreprises du secteur du tabac, a souligné sa contribution à l’économie européenne et a indiqué qu’être “engagée dans une profonde transformation vers un avenir sans tabac”.

“Nous sommes fiers de contribuer au dialogue démocratique et de dialoguer avec tout député européen, quel que soit son groupe politique, qui soit disposé à discuter en s’appuyant sur la science et les faits, ainsi que sur notre détermination à faire partie de la solution”, a déclaré le groupe, qui commercialise également des sachets de nicotine, des cigarettes électroniques et des produits du tabac chauffés.

Débat sur les traités internationaux

L’une des craintes soulevées par Tilly Metz et d’autres députés européens est de savoir si les règles antitabac de l’OMS sont correctement respectées.

Sa Convention-cadre stipule que les politiques de santé publique doivent être protégées contre les intérêts commerciaux de l’industrie du tabac. Elle n’interdit pas le lobbying, mais les lignes directrices relatives à la mise en œuvre du traité précisent que les décideurs politiques doivent limiter leurs interactions avec ce secteur au strict nécessaire aux fins de sa réglementation, et garantir la transparence de ces réunions.

L’industrie affirme qu’elle respecte les règles et expose son point de vue en toute transparence. Elle invoque également un arrêt rendu en 2022 par la Cour de justice de l’Union européenne, selon lequel le traité n’interdit pas sa participation à la mise en œuvre de la lutte antitabac ; il “vise uniquement à empêcher que les politiques de lutte antitabac des parties à la convention ne soient influencées par les intérêts de cette industrie”.

Par ailleurs, le secteur fait valoir que la Convention-cadre de l’OMS ne couvre pas les produits à base de nicotine sans tabac. Ces produits sont particulièrement visés par un durcissement de la réglementation, alors que l’Europe s’apprête à revoir les règles relatives aux produits du tabac et à la publicité, ainsi que les taxes minimales au niveau du continent.

Simon Trussler a assuré que British American Tobacco respecte l’ensemble des réglementations et cela de façon transparente. La Convention-cadre de l’OMS en matière de lutte antitabac a été “mal cité et mal compris”, a-t-il pointé.

L’entreprise a également fait valoir que le champ d’application du traité se limite aux produits fabriqués à partir de feuilles de tabac.

Ce n’est pas la position de l’OMS. Conseillère Europe sur la lutte contre le tabagisme de l’agence onusienne, Kristina Mauer-Stender a souligné que la portée du traité “va au-delà de la simple réduction de la consommation de tabac”.

L’article 5.2.b impose aux parties d’adopter et de mettre en œuvre des mesures législatives et autres efficaces “visant à prévenir et à réduire la consommation de tabac, la dépendance à la nicotine et l’exposition à la fumée de tabac”, a-t-elle détaillé. “Par conséquent, la prévention de la dépendance à la nicotine est un objectif explicite de la mise en œuvre de la Convention, et non une simple considération indirecte.”

Et la même d’ajouter que les décisions de la Conférence des Parties avaient également porté progressivement sur les produits du tabac et à base de nicotine nouveaux et émergents.

Des dates qui coïncident

La publication de ces données sur les réunions des eurodéputées intervient alors que le Parti populaire européen est pointé du doigt pour avoir édulcoré les formulations sur le tabac dans un rapport non contraignant sur les maladies cardiovasculaires publié cet été.

Les élus du PPE ont proposé de modifier la formulation indiquant que la nicotine devait être soumise à la “même” réglementation que le tabac, pour parler plutôt de “règles appropriées”. Cette proposition a été soutenue par deux députées européennes qui figuraient au troisième rang des parlementaires ayant tenu le plus grand nombre de réunions avec les acteurs du secteur : Jessica Polfjärd et Elena Nevado del Campo.

Le rapport final adopté par le Parlement européen reflétait cette proposition.

Romana Jerković, députée européenne du groupe des Socialistes et démocrates, qui a piloté le rapport au sein de la commission de la Santé, avait déclaré à l’époque qu’elle aurait souhaité que celui-ci soit plus ambitieux sur le tabac.

Les activités de lobbying se sont également intensifiées, alors que la Commission européenne s’apprête à publier plusieurs réglementations actualisées concernant les produits du tabac et à base de nicotine.

Selon le Smoke Free Partnership, les pics d’activité en matière de réunions coïncident avec des textes majeurs, comme une directive sur la fiscalité. “Même si les réunions ne suffisent pas à elles seules à prouver une influence directe sur les décisions, elles mettent en évidence les possibilités dont dispose l’industrie pour façonner le débat législatif”, a souligné sa directrice Erin Roman.

La transparence concernant les réunions avec les acteurs du secteur n’est pas suffisante, a estimé Erin Roman, pointant que ces rendez-vous ne devaient avoir lieu que s’ils étaient “strictement nécessaires à une réglementation efficace”.

Pour un autre député européen du groupe des Socialistes et démocrates, le lobbying est allé trop loin.

“Les amendements visant à affaiblir les nouvelles règles relatives aux produits du tabac dans le cadre d’un plan de lutte contre la première cause de mortalité en Europe ne sont pas venus de nulle part : ce sont les groupes rencontrant le plus l’industrie qui sont à l’origine de cet affaiblissement des règles”, a soulevé Nicolás González Casares.

Des réunions surtout avec des élus de droite

Les députés européens qui ont le plus rencontré l’industrie du tabac au cours de cette législature sont pour la plupart issus de la droite.

Auke Zijlstra, des Patriotes, a tenu le plus grand nombre de réunions (14), suivi de Pietro Fiocchi, des CRE (9). Michalis Hadjipantela, Elena Nevado del Campo et Jessica Polfjärd, tous membres du PPE, en ont déclaré 8 chacun.

Auke Zijlstra a précisé qu’il s’entretenait toujours avec les secteurs concernés lorsqu’une proposition législative susceptible de les affecter était à l’étude.

“Je ne pense pas avoir participé à beaucoup de réunions consacrées à la législation sur le tabac et la nicotine. S’intéresser à ce domaine fait partie intégrante de notre métier, et je ne comprends pas les députés européens qui se forgent une opinion sans s’y être penchés”, a-t-il ajouté.

Il a également nié que le secteur soit surreprésenté lors des réunions avec les parlementaires, avant de lancer : “Il y a beaucoup de consommateurs.” Et le même d’encourager les ONG à demander davantage de réunions afin d’exposer leur point de vue.

Le Smoke Free Partnership a déclaré avoir subi une “pression considérable” sur ses ressources en raison de la suppression des subventions de fonctionnement de l’UE l’année dernière. “Nous avons continué à dialoguer avec les décideurs politiques et à coordonner l’expertise indépendante en matière de santé publique, mais la réduction des financements nous oblige à faire des choix difficiles quant aux activités à privilégier”, a indiqué l’ONG, ajoutant qu’il existait un déséquilibre par rapport aux ressources dont dispose l’industrie.

Un porte-parole de Michalis Hadjipantela a relaté que ce dernier collaborait avec un large éventail de parties prenantes, puisqu’il est membre de six commissions. Il “reste totalement indépendant dans ses évaluations et ses décisions”, a précisé le porte-parole, ajoutant : “Le fait de rencontrer une partie prenante n’implique pas pour autant que l’on approuve ses points de vue ou ses intérêts.”

Elena Nevado Del Campo, elle, a expliqué que ses rencontres avec les représentants du secteur du tabac s’expliquaient par le nombre important de producteurs de tabac dans sa région, et qu’elle se devait d’écouter ce secteur, qui est un employeur majeur. Elle a également rencontré des groupes défendant le point de vue opposé. “Je m’engage en faveur d’une Europe en bonne santé et, parallèlement, aux côtés de ces agriculteurs qui se lèvent chaque jour pour travailler les champs d’Estrémadure et dynamiser notre économie régionale.”

Au moment de la publication de cet article, Pietro Fiocchi et Jessica Polfjärd n’avaient pas répondu aux demandes de commentaires.

La fiscalité du paquet

De nombreuses réunions ont porté sur la directive relative à la taxation du tabac, qui est en cours d’examen au sein du Conseil de l’UE. Cette directive fixera des taxes minimales sur la nicotine et les produits du tabac, et élargira la définition des produits concernés.

Parmi les autres sujets abordés lors des réunions et faisant l’objet de déclarations au registre de la transparence figurent les produits du tabac et les directives en matière de publicité, ainsi que la “réduction des risques”. Actuellement, la Commission européenne prépare des révisions des règles relatives aux produits et à la publicité.

Les élus ont déclaré avoir tenu au moins 178 réunions avec des représentants de Philip Morris International (PMI), soit bien plus qu’avec n’importe quel autre fabricant de tabac. British American Tobacco (BAT) arrive en deuxième position, avec 60 réunions.

D’autres données communiquées à POLITICO par Transparency International UE montrent que PMI se classait en quatrième position, derrière Meta, Google et Apple, parmi les entreprises ayant rencontré le plus grand nombre de députés européens et de leurs assistants. Une enquête menée l’année dernière par POLITICO avait révélé que PMI avait également mené avec succès des actions de lobbying auprès de la Commission européenne.

Les données du registre de transparence montrent également quels pays sont les plus enclins à écouter les lobbyistes du tabac.

Les députés européens originaires d’Italie, premier producteur de feuilles de tabac de l’Union, ont rencontré les représentants du secteur bien plus souvent que ceux d’autres nationalités : plus d’une réunion sur cinq avec des représentants de l’industrie du tabac au Parlement a impliqué un élu italien.

Cette situation s’explique en partie par le fait que la société italienne Manifatture Sigaro Toscano a rencontré exclusivement des députés européens italiens. Un peu moins de la moitié des réunions de BAT ont eu lieu avec des députés européens italiens. La Botte était également bien représentée lors des réunions avec PMI, même si les élus allemands ont déclaré avoir rencontré cette entreprise un peu plus souvent.

Ces données collectées par le Smoke Free Partnership, qui s’appuient sur les déclarations des parlementaires concernant leurs rencontres, offrent probablement une image prudente du lobbying de l’industrie du tabac au Parlement européen. POLITICO a supprimé les déclarations contenant des informations insuffisantes, mais a également ajouté les rencontres déclarées plus récemment.

Les géants du tabac s’efforcent globalement d’orienter les consommateurs vers des produits nicotiniques dans le cadre de ce qu’ils qualifient d’approche de “réduction des risques”. Ils affirment que les produits nicotiniques et sans fumée constituent de meilleures alternatives au tabac à fumer et doivent donc être suffisamment attrayants pour que les gens les préfèrent aux cigarettes.

Leurs opposants contestent cet argument, affirmant que les gens n’ont pas besoin d’être exposés à des produits créant une dépendance. Ils soulignent également la forte consommation de sachets de nicotine et d’autres produits similaires chez les jeunes, qui, sans cela, ne fumaient pas.

Au moins 28 réunions figurant dans le jeu de données issues du registre de la transparence faisaient référence à des mesures de santé publique, plutôt qu’à la réglementation ou à la fiscalité du tabac. Et cette liste n’est probablement pas exhaustive, car un grand nombre de descriptions fournies par les participants eux-mêmes restent vagues. Deux réunions ont explicitement mentionné les maladies cardiovasculaires.

Tilly Metz a fait partie d’un groupe d’élus qui ont milité pour restreindre l’accès des lobbyistes du tabac aux députés européens et ont accusé le Parlement de ne pas respecter ses obligations au titre de la Convention-cadre de l’OMS pour la lutte antitabac. Mais cette initiative a échoué en juin dernier.

Tilly Metz a assuré qu’elle “continuerai[t] à se battre” pour que le Parlement européen respecte pleinement le cadre réglementaire relatif au tabac.

Cet article a d’abord été publié par POLITICO en anglais, puis a été édité en français par Jean-Christophe Catalon.

Germany should become a “sovereign AI nation” by 2030 and narrow the gap with leading AI hubs in the U.S. and China, according to a report drafted by the government’s AI task force and obtained by POLITICO set to be released Monday.

“The next 12 to 18 months will therefore be decisive in setting the course,” read the report, which was due to be presented to the National Security Council and also at a summit on AI in Berlin.

Germany wants to secure access to the world’s leading models while strengthening European alternatives, particularly through expanded cooperation with France and Canada, according to the report. 

“We are leveraging collaborations with like-minded partners in the EU and worldwide (especially France and Canada) to benefit the German AI ecosystem and ensure sovereign access,” the report noted. “We will also use intra-European collaborations,” such as with French AI company Mistral, “to achieve this leverage,” its authors added.

At the same time, “AI made in Germany” should stand out through its focus on industrial AI with “highly specialized models,” the report read.

“A key focus here is the development of innovative production systems to increase productivity through the use of AI,” the report noted. “The widespread use of AI and AI-based robotics can boost productivity and quality, optimize industrial processes, and improve control over complex systems.”

To help speed up the development of AI in Germany, the government plans to act as a “strategic anchor customer,” using public contracts and pilot projects to help European AI providers enter the market.

The plan comes as Germany struggles to catch up on AI while cultivating more strategic autonomy in the area. Much of the blueprint, however, lacks key details, including on financing. The measures “neither constitute funding decisions nor prejudge” future budget procedures, according to the report.

The government established the task force in June to better coordinate AI initiatives across several ministries. The blueprint proposes 18 measures such as plans to “strategically expand AI computing infrastructure and connect it as a European ecosystem” as well as “strengthening the semiconductor value chain.”

By 2030, the government wants at least 80% of large companies and 55% of small and medium-size businesses to use AI. Berlin is also aiming for 90% of federal agencies to have at least one AI application in production. AI agents are expected to prepare administrative processes “end to end” and, where legally permitted, complete them with full automation. 

The government is also working to increase the country’s AI data center capacity by 300% compared with 2025, the report read.

Jasper Bennink contributed reporting.

]]> en Europe’s supermarkets hit by new wave of cyberattacks targeting fridges https://www.politico.eu/article/new-supermarket-hack-in-belgium-sweden-luxembourg/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Mon, 02 Nov 2026 11:19:32 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9254550 BRUSSELS — Refrigerators in dozens of supermarkets in at least five EU countries were out of service on Monday, local news outlets reported, in what appears to be a repeat of cyberattacks that hit French stores last month.

As of Monday afternoon, there were news reports of incidents affecting supermarkets in Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands and Estonia. 

Several store managers told local media that refrigerator temperatures suddenly spiked to up to 50 degrees Celsius. This mirrors the French incidents last month, in which attackers appeared to remotely manipulate the fridges’ defrosting mechanisms so that they overheated.

It’s not confirmed that the attacks are connected or used the same software vulnerabilities that hit French chains, though one supermarket spokesperson said the incident is a cyberattack “similar to the one in France.”

Ken Munro, a cybersecurity researcher, said in an interview that supermarkets should have disconnected their refrigerators and the devices used to monitor and remotely manage them from the Internet. “I don’t accept any other excuse … particularly in light of the earlier [attacks in France],” he said.

Inti De Ceukelaire, another cyber researcher, also said the incident suggests supermarkets did not take the necessary steps even after the France attacks. “It seems that some of them simply did not get patched, which is quite ridiculous,” he said.

Belgian media reported on Monday morning that temperatures in supermarket refrigerators had suddenly spiked, forcing them to throw food away. A spokesperson for the Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium said the agency is “closely” following the incident, adding that the attackers are unknown and that it “may never be possible to identify them.”

John Billow, director of Sweden’s National Cyber Security Centre, told POLITICO that there are “similarities” to the French incidents and that the agency is in touch with affected organizations. A European Commission spokesperson said it’s aware of the incidents and is using the EU-Cyclone network to coordinate and share information.

Following France

French supermarkets were hit with a wave of similar incidents in mid-October, when attackers targeted refrigerators by Danfoss, a Danish manufacturer of store fridges. Danfoss did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The attacks in France triggered a response from the country’s prime minister and its cybersecurity agency.

Belgian supermarket chain Delhaize alerted its store managers early on Monday morning of problems with refrigerators, and Belgian broadcaster RTBF cited a store manager as saying that the problems were due to a cyberattack like those in France.

A spokesperson for the company said it is aware of an “IT incident affecting the refrigeration systems in a number of Delhaize stores.” A spokesperson for Colruyt, which operates Spar stores in Belgium, said in a statement that fridges in “around five” Spar stores have been affected. “We are currently doing everything we can to resolve the issue,” they said, adding that no Colruyt stores have been affected. 

A Carrefour spokesperson confirmed that 15 of its 700 stores have been affected, and that none of its larger “hypermarket” stores are among them. All stores remain open, they said.

Stores in Sweden have also been hit. A spokesperson for supermarket chain ICA confirmed an “incident overnight affecting a small number of ICA stores operating outside ICA’s central network” which affected its fridges and freezers. 

A Coop spokesperson said seven of its 800 stores were affected but the situation, which is “contained and under control.” In one case, a refrigeration system began to generate heat, they said. Last month in France, the attacks caused at least one fire.

Like the public authorities, cyber researchers are looking for signs of who may be responsible. The fact that the attacks have happened again is evidence to suggest a hostile nation could be behind the attacks rather than young hacker pranksters, De Ceukelaire said. Munro, however, said he believes a “copycat” is behind Monday’s attacks.

“This won’t be the end of it,” Munro added. “There will be more.”

]]> en King mulls De Wever’s resignation as Belgian budget talks fail https://www.politico.eu/article/belgian-government-in-crisis-over-failed-budget-talks/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Mon, 02 Nov 2026 08:58:14 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9254352 BRUSSELS— Belgium’s King Philippe is considering Prime Minister Bart De Wever’s resignation after the premier offered to step down following failed attempts by his coalition government to agree to plug a €10 billion budget gap.

In an 11th-hour attempt to reach a deal for next year’s budget, top officials from De Wever’s five-party government gathered over the weekend, but left without an agreement early Monday morning. Tuesday was widely seen as the unofficial deadline to strike a deal, as the budget still has to pass through parliament before the end of the year.

As part of the talks, De Wever wanted to show financial markets that Belgium is on track to meet its European obligations. Belgium had a deficit of 5.2 % of GDP in 2025, which is expected to rise further next year.

After De Wever offered his resignation Monday morning, the palace said the king was “postponing his decision” and “will begin consultations tomorrow with the party leaders of the various coalition partners.” It added that the king “is appealing to everyone’s sense of responsibility and urges all stakeholders to prioritize the general interest and a spirit of compromise.”

The prime minister is expected to meet the king again on Friday.

De Wever had ruled out starting the new year with a temporary budget, which would let the government continue with the same budget as last year’s.

Budget talks have been ongoing for weeks, with tensions emerging mostly between the Flemish socialists of Forward and the Francophone center-right Reformist Movement.

The former asked for more contributions from the highest incomes, through taxes, while the latter ruled that out and pushed back against a wider reform of value-added tax.

There were still “far too many taxes on the table,” David Clarinval, deputy prime minister for the Reformist Movement, told reporters when talks broke up. He didn’t rule out discussions resuming today.

Last November, Belgium’s budget talks also went into extra time. On this occasion, De Wever did not tender his resignation, but requested an extension to budget talks from King Philippe. The king granted him an additional 50 days to reach an agreement.

If Belgium is on track for snap elections, the country could lean toward extreme parties, with both the far-right Vlaams Belang and the far-left Workers Party performing well in the polls.

European allies fear a Republican loss could spur President Donald Trump to dramatically step up his attacks on the alliance, according to five NATO diplomats, all of whom were granted anonymity to speak freely on the sensitive issue.

Their worry is that if he is restrained by Congress on domestic policy, Trump, as commander-in-chief of the U.S. military, may seek to cement his legacy on foreign affairs, where he has a freer hand. That could mean pulling thousands more troops out of Europe, three of the diplomats said.

“Usually what happens to lame duck presidents is a mix of venting frustrations and adventurism in foreign policy,” said one senior European defense official. And attacking NATO “seems to be a consistent part of [the] Trump worldview.”

White House Assistant Press Secretary Olivia Wales told POLITICO that “President Trump has done more for NATO than anyone else,” citing his successes in securing agreements by allies to raise defense spending to 5% of GDP by 2035, bolster U.S. military presence in Greenland, and efforts to end Russia’s all-out war in Ukraine.

Yet he “remains firm that our NATO allies should have been there for the United States” over the war in Iran, she said, adding: “The President will never settle for the West’s managed decline and will continue to unapologetically advance our interests at home and abroad.”

Democrats are widely expected to win the House of Representatives and potentially flip the Senate, while Trump’s personal approval ratings have fallen to his lowest on record.

The worries underscore growing transatlantic tensions after a U.S. cutoff of Starlink satellite services for Ukraine and a fresh rapprochement between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin weeks before the midterms. Further attacks would deal a fresh blow to NATO, just as Russia steps up its sabotage campaign and so-called hybrid war across Europe.

“He could be very pissed off,” said one of the NATO diplomats. If so, “he’ll be very harsh.”

Forces, money and Ukraine

At the heart of the concerns is an upcoming review of U.S. forces in Europe, expected by December. If Trump is blocked from legislating domestically, he may seek to significantly increase the scope of that pullback to rally his MAGA base, three of the diplomats said. 

The president could also decide to tie continued American presence on the continent to Europe accepting a U.S.-backed peace deal in Ukraine, said Oana Lungescu, a former NATO official and distinguished fellow at the Royal United Services Institute think tank.

“There is a risk that all these things — the U.S. force posture review, Ukraine, European security order … somehow are treated as part of a much bigger deal with Putin,” she said, “creating a very dangerous situation for security in Europe.”

Trump could also move to cut U.S. contributions to the alliance’s common funding, limit the NATO-backed PURL arms-buying scheme for Ukraine, as well as deepen ties still further with Russia, the diplomats said.

A major electoral defeat for the Republicans could also spell big changes at the Pentagon, which would have knock-on effects for any plans currently being hatched in the building.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has become a deeply unpopular figure in Congress, given his refusal to provide regular briefings about budgets and operations to lawmakers, especially Democrats.

That unpopularity has led to speculation that Hegseth could be out after an electoral blowout for Trump, partially because a Democrat-led Congress would slap Hegseth with probes into his firing of dozens of generals and admirals with no cause, and the faltering war with Iran. Those hearings and investigations would hamstring Hegseth and his team, and could prove embarrassing for the administration.

If Hegseth does move on, there would be a transition period in the Pentagon which could push any decisions about moving U.S. troops out of Europe back by weeks or months.

In theory, a Democrat majority in the House and Senate would restrain Trump’s maneuverability even on foreign and defense issues, even if U.S. law currently imposes a minimum limit of 76,000 on troop presence in Europe. 

But “it is doubtful that at least the troop floors would stand up to legal scrutiny and in any case Trump has been very willing to ignore the courts,” said Jennifer Kavanagh, a senior fellow at the Defense Priorities think tank. “The Trump administration has regularly ignored funding guidance from Congress, spending money on activities the legislative branch has not authorized.”

If Trump decides to impose a more sprawling drawdown, Europe will have “the most trouble” replacing assets including electronic warfare capabilities, air defense systems, intelligence and reconnaissance support, aerial refueling, and some types of logistics, she said.

Other allies are more skeptical Trump would hammer NATO. “We have had speculations all the time about Trump … coming out of the NATO; this has not happened so far,” Montenegrin Defense Minister Dragan Krapović told POLITICO. “Congress is the one making the decision, the final decision about less troops in Europe.”

But “to make assumptions with a high probability of success needs an object of study that makes rational decisions,” said a sixth NATO diplomat. “I don’t think we are there with the current POTUS.”

NATO and the U.S. Department of Defense did not respond to requests for comment by POLITICO.

“There’s a lot of traumatised people in Brussels” from the Brexit process, said Kallas. 

“There is no doubt that leaving the EU cost our economy and we’re not as strong as we might have been,” started Streeting.

Karol Nawrocki had even turned back mid-flight from a planned visit to Senegal and went into the Tribunal’s building, pushing aside a judge who had blocked the door.

Together with his own guards and aides, Nawrocki stayed in the premises until the early morning hours, as a few thousand protesters camped outside.

And leaving in the morning, he thanked them for having “defended the Polish constitution.”

The events unfolded amid a clash between the centre-right prime minister Donald Tusk and the rightwing opposition party, Law and Justice (PiS), supporting Nawrocki, over the status of judges in the country’s highest court.

And the PiS party’s approach to the situation was “designed to heighten perceptions of existential political conflict and mobilise supporters,” while making Tusk look like part of an unaccountable elite, said Roch Dunin-Wąsowicz, a politics professor at University College London.

Natasza Styczyńska, a scholar of European studies at the Jagiellonian University in Kraków, also told EUobserver that the courtroom melodrama was meant to “strengthen the image” of PiS ahead of next year’s parliamentary election, which falls due by 11 November.

]]> Scandal-hit EU innovation agency disputes auditors’ finding that €8.7m may be unrecoverable https://euobserver.com/246128/scandal-hit-eu-innovation-agency-disputes-auditors-finding-that-e8-7m-may-be-unrecoverable/ Mon, 02 Nov 2026 16:46:47 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246128 The European Institute of Innovation & Technology is under renewed scrutiny after an audit suggested “a material level of error” and flagged that it could fail to recover €8.7m from its beneficiaries. This comes after several investigations into the agency were launched in recent years.]]> The European Institute of Innovation & Technology (EIT), which received €435m in taxpayer money in 2025, is the only EU agency out of a total of 43 whose accounts did not yield a “clean opinion” in the most-recent audit.

The accounts of the innovation hub did not properly reflect an €8.7m recovery uncertainty, according to a report by European Court of Auditors (ECA) last week.

Several dozen of its auditors check the EU agencies every year to form a basis for Brussels bodies to later make decisions on funding.

The financial audit delivers the latest blow to the EIT, an EU agency whose bodies have faced several investigations over spending.

“Taxpayers should be concerned,” said Kenneth Haar, researcher at Corporate Europe Observatory, a watchdog. “I find it amazing and worrying to see the EIT house is still not in order, though it was more than two years ago that investigators first stepped in.”

Lead ECA auditor Petri Sarvamaa said, “The good news is that public money is managed well overall. But the weaknesses we identified also show why strong checks are essential in protecting EU taxpayers’ money.”

Based in Budapest, the EIT aims to boost European competitiveness by connecting enterprises, researchers and education.

It distributes funds to sector-specific partnerships called knowledge and innovation communities (KICs). And the spending habits of some of these KICs have caused a financial and reputational headache for EIT bosses.

Agency disputes €8.7m figure

The ECA’s report of the EIT’s financial accounts published on Thursday (29 October) said the innovation hub’s grant payments were affected by “a material level of error”.

But because verification checks were incomplete, it “could not provide an estimated error rate” of grant payments.

The report also flagged that the agency could fail to recover €8.7m. At least some of this is due to EIT Manufacturing, a KIC which filed for liquidation in March 2026.

The audit states: “An impairment should have been recognised […] EIT receivables and net assets are overstated by €8.7m, impairment expenses are understated by the same amount, and the economic result for the year is overstated by €8.7m.”

But the innovation and tech agency disagreed with these findings.

While the EIT acknowledged that an impairment should have been recognised, it told auditors the amount is actually up to €0.5m, not €8.7m. The chance of recovering the money, the EIT said, is “very likely”.

Specifically, it expects to recover €5.9m via the so-called Mutual Insurance Mechanism (MIM), and €2.3m by offsetting money owed by EIT Manufacturing.

The court of auditors also said risks are “amplified” by the use of multiannual grants reported and cleared only every 18 months. In response, the EIT said it is moving to 12-month reporting periods.

“I think this is all about the pitfalls of letting private actors handle public money, and with relatively few strings attached…. it invites the sort of trouble we have seen,” added Haar.

“At another level, I believe it is a symptom of the laissez-faire approach of the EU institutions to start-ups and innovation.”

Read more

EU’s Horizon-suspension sanction for Israel ‘a bad joke’, says Borrell

Pumped up KICs?

EU law sets out that in their seventh year, KICs should be subject to scrutiny before they can receive another seven years of taxpayer money.

They are envisioned to become financially independent and sustainable after 15 years of existence.

In 2025, the digital, clean energy, and climate change KICs were due to be independent as they reached their 15th birthdays. 

But in 2026-27 two of them reportedly received a shared total of €43m from the EIT, which pumped up KICs with EU funds past the supposed expiration date.

First touching land after having survived a sail aboard an overcrowded dinghy in a storm, 28 migrants were trooped through a sped-up "tick-boxing" screening, which experts worry will not accurately measure the vulnerabilities they're up against. ]]> The survivors of a recent maritime migrant rescue operation carried out by the German NGO SOS Humanity were screened on the port docks as they first set foot on EU soil, revealing the insensitive efficiency at the centre of the EU’s new Pact on Migration and Asylum.

    Read more

    How the rescue of 28 people from a makeshift dinghy in a stormy Mediterranean unfolded – exposing the lethal reality of EU border policy

    The reception policies from the pact, implemented in June 2026, require an initial screening of new EU arrivals to last a maximum of seven days. 

    The 28 survivors rescued from an overcrowded dinghy on a stormy night in the central Mediterranean were disembarked at 11 am on Saturday (31 October), and had finished being processed by the evening.

    Under the new pact, that means their asylum decision will have been most likely conducted then and there. 

    The platform alongside the Humanity 1 vessel was bustling with hazmat suits and police. In the northern Italian port of Livorno, a makeshift processing centre was set up to host the Red Cross’s health scan, the EU agency for asylum’s vulnerability scan and legal information session, as well as the police’s interrogation – all to be carried out within hours of migrants’ stunned arrival.

    “Immediately after a rescue, when people only need to rest, they sit through a compressed screening for authorities to rush through a tick-boxing exercise,” said Marta [the NGO requests only first names are used by journalists], SOS Humanity’s protection officer, as survivors from the ship’s rescue were being disembarked by authorities.

    She had prepared vulnerability certificates for those most in need, in the hope their case be treated with more care. 

    “Some border interrogations can become violent, a person has just disembarked and they are suddenly facing hours of interrogations,” Marta told EUobserver. She has often seen armed Frontex or Europol officers standing along the ship at port, towering over migrants in their most vulnerable hours.

    The new pact on migration foresees police registration into Eurodac, a database set up to share information with other member states, followed by an immediate decision as to whether a newcomer should qualify for an accelerated asylum procedure. 

    That means those from nationalities less likely to be granted asylum would receive an answer within 12 weeks, and are most probably going to be rejected.

    Read more

    ‘Let me die’: tortured migrants and rescue ships face off against EU-sponsored Libyan forces

    “There’s no way you can do an accurate screening of all the traumas someone on this journey has lived in 10 minutes with a police officer,” she added.

Catalogue it under “fiction”, writes Edward Lucas.]]> Since the late 1940s, a clique of influential Americans has hijacked their country’s foreign policy to settle personal and family grudges, using Ukraine as a weapon. The result, as avoidable as it was predictable, has been the disaster of Russia’s invasion.

    That is the argument put forward by Stephen Kinzer in Boiling Point: How America brought war to Ukraine.

    He opens with the disastrous clandestine operations that started in 1949, aimed at supporting the underground anti-communist resistance in Ukraine and other countries.

    They were the work of Frank Wisner, a CIA boss traumatised by witnessing the communist seizure of power in Romania. Other villains include Zbigniew Brzezinski (the son of a Polish diplomat), Madelaine Albright (daughter of a Czechoslovak one) and Victoria Nuland, who has family roots in Moldova and (by marriage) Lithuania.

    Like the others, Kinzer argues, “she imbibed anti-Russian passion with her mother’s milk”.

    These sentiments fuelled what Kinzer calls “the inter-agency” – a self-selecting, powerful group of US government officials, fixated on using their country’s foreign policy as a “cudgel” against the Kremlin.

    ]]>         Zelensky stalls on his EU promises to protect gay rights, even as Ukraine rushes through minority-languages law https://euobserver.com/245901/zelensky-stalls-on-his-eu-promises-to-protect-gay-rights-even-as-ukraine-rushes-through-minority-languages-law/ Mon, 02 Nov 2026 11:05:07 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=245901 Zelensky’s government has shown it can move at lightning speed to please EU partners on some minority rights, yet same-sex partnership and hate-crime bills remain stuck in the Ukrainian parliament.]]> Two months before Kherson was liberated in November 2022, Russian soldiers searched a young shop assistant’s home and found two flags: one Ukrainian, one rainbow.

    In testimony published in July by the United Nations and the Ukrainian rights group Projector, the woman, identified by the pseudonym Olena, described being dragged away, beaten, and threatened with sexual violence. Her captors demanded the names of other LGBTI people in the city. At the time of publication, she had not reported any of this to Ukrainian law enforcement.

    On 12 October, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky signed a national human rights strategy that, for the first time, devoted a section of its own to LGBTI rights. It identifies LGBTI people as a group at heightened risk and commits the state to fighting discrimination and hate crimes. The strategy is tied to Ukraine’s bid to join the European Union. The cabinet has six months to draw up an implementation plan.

    Read more

    Attacks on LGBTI people are the warning sign of a wider backlash against democracy

    I have watched my country make promises like this before. The decree replaces a strategy that Zelensky signed in 2021. The hate crimes bill introduced that year never reached a vote and was withdrawn in 2025. I want to know what will make this promise any different.

    Parliament acted on another question of minority rights that same day. Hungary had blocked two clusters of Ukraine’s accession talks until Kyiv expanded schooling in EU languages for national minorities.

    Those minorities deserve protection. What struck me was how quickly Parliament could provide it. The bill was introduced at the start of October, passed and signed on 12 October. The next day, the EU opened the two clusters.

    Meanwhile, progress on LGBTI rights has been much slower, despite the EU’s equality benchmarks.

    A registered-partnerships bill for same-sex and different-sex couples, introduced in March 2023, has sat in the legal policy committee ever since.

    A bill adding sexual orientation and gender identity to the criminal code’s hate crime provisions has been in committee since August 2025.

    And Ukraine’s own EU roadmap, adopted in May 2025, set the third quarter of that year as the target for passing partnership legislation – the deadline came and went without a vote.

    In February, the Supreme Court let stand a ruling recognising two men as a family, rejecting a challenge from a conservative campaign group. Two months later, Parliament voted 254 to 2 to advance a new Civil Code reserving, de facto, family unions to a man and a woman.

    Rights groups warn that the wording could prevent similar rulings. The speaker has since submitted amendments restoring the current definition of family. Parliament has yet to vote on them.

    When hate crimes become hooliganism

    These failures matter when someone goes to the police to report an attack. In May, after a rally in Ivano-Frankivsk against the Civil Code, men from a “traditional values” counter-event followed the LGBTI activist Olena Shevchenko and a colleague, knocked them down, and stole their posters.

    There was one success, though, back in 2022. Participants adopted the Kunming-Montreal framework, with clear targets: restoring at least 30 percent of degraded ecosystems by 2030, and providing 20 billion dollars a year in financial aid to developing countries.

    So what did countries actually agree on? First, they agreed on the diagnosis I just mentioned: that countries are behind on their 2030 goals. That alone was already a fight.

    Women make up 19.5 percent of information and communication technology specialists in the EU. Start-ups with at least one woman founder receive 12 percent of venture capital.

    Women face greater exposure to AI taking over their tasks, are less represented among the people who build the systems, and are under-financed as founders.

    Our task force within the Connecting Women in Digital Forum asked a narrow question: where does AI policy risk leaving women out, and which instruments already in motion could change that?

    We found five gaps

    Nobody has defined a good AI job. The EUCommission could do so, across wages, security, autonomy, progression and voice, in the Quality Jobs Act due later this year.

    Member states also have until 2 December to transpose the Platform Work Directive, whose safeguards on algorithmic management are a ready model they can choose to extend beyond platform work.

    Transition support follows territories, while AI exposure follows tasks. An administrative worker in a region with no designated just transition territory gets nothing. The next EU budget could make occupational exposure an eligibility trigger, with recipients reported by sex.

    European support for women founders stops at a €75,000 grant. Nothing covers the step from there to €2m. The Commission’s Startup and Scaleup Strategy does not even name that gap; the only one it acknowledges sits above €100m. The Action Plan for women in research, innovation and start-ups, still to be adopted, should include a dedicated facility.

    Digital Decade reporting counts adoption, not who benefits. Every AI indicator should be paired with a result reported by sex, starting with the December revision of the national roadmaps.

    The fifth gap is procurement and it sits at the centre of a debate the EU is already having.

    Read more

    Revealed: New data shows Big Tech lobbying pushing EU towards sweeping data-protection rollback

    Europe’s conversation about technological sovereignty usually begins with infrastructure: compute, chips, cloud and data centres. Sovereignty is also produced through purchasing: public contracts decide which suppliers gain revenue, references, scale and credibility.

    In concentrated AI and cloud markets, one significant public contract is often what qualifies a firm to compete for the next.

    Public procurement accounts for around 14 percent of EU gross domestic product. The commission’s proposal for a Public Procurement Act, tabled on 9 September, treats that spending explicitly as strategy: simpler rules, but also environmental, social, innovation, security and resilience considerations, and a European preference.

    It tracks awards to small and medium-sized enterprises, but it does not track awards to women-led firms.

    Start counting the women

    The Cloud and AI Development Act, tabled in June, repeats the pattern: Article 33 requires member states to monitor cloud and AI procurement for barriers facing smaller firms and to report annually on their share of contracts, but it says nothing about gender.

    Adding women-led firms to that reporting requirement would begin to show who is actually winning Europe’s cloud and AI business.

    Procurement data is not currently broken down by technology category or supplier ownership, so policymakers can count contract value without knowing who got the opportunity.

    In one version of sovereignty, Europe could spend more public money on AI and end up reinforcing a concentrated supplier market. In another version, public demand could deliberately broaden the range of firms that can build and scale technology in Europe.

    Both count as European procurement in the statistics, yet they do not produce the same market.

    Importantly, no one needs to wait for the new Act. Article 67  permits contracting authorities to use award criteria linked to the subject matter of the contract, while Article 70 allows conditions governing contract performance. That means a contracting authority can, for example, assess the inclusiveness of the team delivering a contract, where that criterion is sufficiently linked to the contract itself, or require prime contractors to report the share of subcontracted value going to women-led firms.

    Spain has legislated equality criteria across every phase of procurement in its science system, and the European Institute for Gender Equality publishes a methodology. The new Act should add a duty to report awards to women-led firms by number and value, so policymakers can see whether those options are actually being used.

    AI does not need a separate equality regime.

    Each gap we identified can be addressed through an instrument already in force or on the table.

    What is missing is not another framework, but action and political will power. So our ask to EU institutions, and to the governments now transposing, budgeting and negotiating these files, is simple: pick one of the five gaps, name the instrument that can close it, and name who in your institution can act on it immediately.

    Representatives from European rights forums, culture groups and a journalism federation gathered in a bid to keep enough money flowing to their organisations.

    “There’s a very grim future if we continue with these cuts,” said Rhys Nugent of Culture Action Europe, one of the protest’s organisers. “These sectors are already on their knees.”

    The demonstration came after EU leaders discussed giving less money than previously proposed to AgoraEU, an umbrella for culture, media, democracy and rights initiatives, within the EU’s 2028-2034 budget.

    30% less for culture

    Reacting to the EU Commission’s proposal to give AgoraEU €8.6bn under the long-term budget, the EU parliament’s budget committee asked to ramp this up to €10.7bn.

    But national capitals have not agreed to either proposal.

    Instead, the Irish presidency of Council presented a plan earlier this month (October 10) to allocate €5.3bn for AgoraEU –  representing a 30 percent cut to the commission’s proposal. It was responding to pressures for frugality from some member states.

    National capitals are yet to finalise a budget agreement.

    Read more

    Pressure mounts on EU leaders to strike a budget deal by December

    “They picked culture because they think it’s an easy target, but it will affect journalists, artists and NGOs who are the backbone of our democratic society” said Nela Reihl, a German Green MEP and chair of parliament’s culture and education committee.

    “If this goes through, people will wake up one day and ask: why are my rights not protected? Why has that film festival disappeared? Where has my local publisher gone?” she said.

    “These cuts will save only a tiny percent of the EU budget but cause massive damage to these sectors,” added the German lawmaker. 

    What could be chopped?

    AgoraEU is a new umbrella for Creative Europe and Citizens, Equality, Rights and Values (CERV).

    Protest organiser Nugent said Creative Europe “funds everything from small theatrical productions to large cooperation around Europe.”

    He pointed to Flow, an Oscar-winning film, Europa Cinemas, and Culture Moves Europe as examples of the types of bodies that could be affected by a lack of EU funding.

What's in them?]]> One could ask, what might politicians from a far-right party — as the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution describes Alternative for Germany (AfD), write to one another?

    More than 400,000 emails exchanged by AfD members between March 2013 and September 2026, effectively covering the party’s entire history, have appeared online.

    They were published by hackers from the Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoSecrets) organisation, who obtained 284 gigabytes of data, including minutes from meetings of the party leadership, payslips, strategic documents, membership lists and donors’ names.

    AfD and its enemies

    According to the Correctiv website, the material also includes election campaign plans, for example for the 2025 parliamentary election. Their authors describe how to reach potential voter groups. They describe the governing parties at the time as enemies.

    It is unclear yet whether all the emails are genuine, but the party has confirmed the leak. German media outlets with access to them estimate that assessing the information could take months.

    It is already clear that the emails offer an insight into how Germany’s currently strongest political party operates and how it approaches certain issues, including neo-Nazism.

    The media are gradually uncovering messages that are uncomfortable for AfD’s leading figures, including its co-chair Alice Weidel.

    One of the most striking findings is that in private she was not as radical as she liked to portray herself in public. And, according to German media, the difference is considerable.

    The leaked emails also suggest how the German party sought to forge closer ties with the US conservative Maga movement and president Donald Trump, whom it saw as a potential ally.

    In foreign policy, they also point to deeper links with Russia than had previously been known.

    Thousands of emails could also play a role in a potential ban on the party, which is not yet decided upon but is being debated in Berlin.

    So what have they revealed?

    What had not previously been known about relations with Russia

I will not go back there.”

    The 25 year old Nigerian man is one of many rescued by the German NGO SOS Humanity on Tuesday (27 October) to have escaped living hell in Libya, at the hands of a regime paid by the EU to keep migrants away from its borders.

    “I was in prison for one year, for no reason,” said Sulaiman, whose name has been changed to preserve his anonymity. “Any time in the morning they come to distribute food, there are beatings. No one lets you go without a beating,” he told EUobserver.

    Every day he’d subsist on one small slice of bread in “a cage for 100 people, where there are all skeletons,” he described with tears in his eyes. 

    Sulaiman had tried to leave Libya twice before on small boats, but each time he’d been pulled back to land by violent militias, one of whom he described to be an ‘official’ authority. 

    Data from the International Organisation for migration (IOM) and the UN found over 200,000 people to have been illegally intercepted in the central Mediterranean and returned to Libya since 2016. 

    Read more

    And like many other search and rescue organisations, SOS Humanity’s own work has been significantly impeded by Libyan groups – whether they be the so-called Libyan coast guard or paramilitary groups known for hijacking small migrant boats in open sea to rob everyone on board and pull them back to illegal detention facilities.

    Men, women, families with children, and unaccompanied minors alike are kept in prisons until they can pay their way out.

    “I lied, and told my family I was in Tunisia,” a young boy from Sudan told EUobserver. 

    “I knew my mother couldn’t take it, knowing what would be happening to me in Libya,” he said, after having been rescued by SOS Humanity alongside 27 others in the early hours of Tuesday. He is one of 11 children aboard traveling alone.

    ]]>         Listen: Why is the EU introducing a new €2 charge on parcels? https://euobserver.com/245922/listen-why-is-the-eu-introducing-a-new-e2-charge-on-parcels/ Fri, 30 Oct 2026 09:36:20 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=245922 From this Sunday, the EU is imposing a new €2 charge on parcels coming from outside the bloc. It comes on top of the €3 charge on small parcels announced in June.]]>

    Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

    EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

    Find the full transcript below:

    From this Sunday, the EU is imposing a new €2 charge on parcels coming from outside the bloc. It comes on top of the €3 charge on small parcels announced in June.

    So why is the EU doing this, and what difference will it make? Let’s start with what’s changing.

    From this Sunday, there will be a €2 tax on each product category contained in a parcel coming from outside the EU. This ads up to the €3 tax on small parcels introduced in June this year. So for a parcel of less than €150, you can already count a €5 charge, and that’s if your parcel contains just one category of item.

    Say you order four different garments from the Chinese platform Shein. The total charge comes to €20.

    Officially, it’s the sellers who are supposed to pay, not consumers. But in practice, they pass the cost on to customers one way or another.

    So why this second charge? The €3 charge adopted in June was meant to tackle the flood of small parcels coming from companies like Temu and Shein.

    Parcels of very low value, often just a few euros. And that’s not an exaggeration. According to Kristian Vanderwaeren, Belgium’s head of customs, the average value of a parcel before the charge was around €5. And that’s an average, so imagine the number of parcels worth less than €5 that literally come from the other side of the world.

    Read more

    Listen: Who will benefit from the new €3 tax on small parcels?

    Until now, parcels worth less than €150 were exempt from customs duties. That was a big hole in customs revenue. And at the same time, customs officers had more and more parcels to process. Hence the €3 levy.

    Now the new charge is different. It applies to all parcels, not just the smallest ones. Its goal is to raise revenue to cover the cost of checks. Because if the EU wants to fight fraud and make sure products on the market are safe, customs controls have to increase. And that takes time, and therefore money.

    We don’t know yet exactly how much the new tax will bring in revenues. What we know, even if the situation is not comparable, is what the €3 tax is starting to bring.

    Between June and September, the €3 charge brought in €364mln for Belgian customs. In just three months.

    Belgium is a major entry point for parcels bound for the EU, through the port of Antwerp and Liège airport. So we cannot duplicate that figure for other EU countries.

    Read more

    EU ‘open’ to curbs on imports of Chinese chemicals and machinery, after hybrid-car deal

    Still, over a full year, the two charges combined, on top of standard customs duties, should raise a significant amount. We can therefore imagine that countries outside the EU are not happy, especially China.

    Beijing describes the measure as protectionist. It also argues that the cost will largely be passed on to European consumers, which means, in its view, that the EU is shooting itself in the foot.

    But that is, to some extent, exactly what Europeans are hoping for. If Chinese products become more expensive, they become less attractive.

    Business groups agree. Comeos, the Belgian federation for trade and services, welcomed the charge as a response to unfair competition.

    Think about an everyday product worth less than €100. There is usually a big price gap between the Chinese version and the one made in Europe. When that gap is somewhere between €5 and €20, the charge can tip the balance. It may push you to buy local, or not to buy at all. In both case, this means less money getting out of the EU.

    And there are already signs it’s working. Since the €3 charge came in in June, the volume of small parcels arriving at Liège airport has dropped by 60 percent.

    The European consumer organisation BEUC has also welcomed the move, saying more border controls mean safer products.

    Something that is not immediately visible for citizens, but which has its importance.

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/01/us-china-trade-war-trump-xi</link>
      <description><p>A truce has cooled the trade conflict, but neither country has done anything to limit the outbreak of new hostilities</p><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a>’s trade wars have largely fallen off the headlines. Fears of new tariffs flare up from time to time when the US president goes off the rails – for instance, threatening to end US trade with countries with which it has a deficit unless the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/federal-reserve">Federal Reserve</a> cuts interest rates. But the sense that the world’s two largest economies are plowing ahead into an overt economic conflagration has taken a back seat to other, more salient fears, about Trump ending American democracy, AI killing us all and stuff like that.</p><p>The sense of calm is misleading. Under the radar, the world is marching toward an economic war of potentially epic proportions, one that, history suggests, could well spill over into the real thing.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/01/us-china-trade-war-trump-xi">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/oct/30/tech-stocks-drop-earnings-report</link>
      <description><p>Big tech stocks falter as investors question whether billions being poured into AI can generate returns quickly enough</p><p>A sell-off of tech stocks that began earlier this month and gained steam with disappointing earnings from leading tech companies drove US markets down by hundreds of billions of dollars Friday. In total, the decline has knocked nearly $1tn in value off the tech-heavy Nasdaq exchange in one week and erased about $2tn in a month.</p><p>The S&amp;P 500, the index of the 500 most valuable companies in the US, fell by more than 1% Friday, losing hundreds of billions of dollars in market value. It was on track to erase its gain for October, even though it set its all-time high during the same month. The weakness for technology stocks dragged the Nasdaq composite down even further, more than 3%, also erasing hundreds of billions in value.       <description><p>A layoff and a leap of faith convinced Katie Teixeira she had what it takes to run her own business</p><p>In 2010, Katie Teixeira adopted a kitten found all alone in an abandoned house. The kitten – so tiny she fit in the palm of Teixeira’s hand – needed to be bottle-fed every few hours. For weeks, Teixeira set her alarm for middle-of-the-night feedings and drove home on her lunch break to care for the kitten she named Milo. As the cat grew, so did the connection between them.</p><p>“We just bonded,” Teixeira says. “Like mother and daughter.”</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/apr/24/pet-memorial-jewelry-small-business">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>It is essential not just to fund the public goods the nation needs, it is indispensable to restore a sense of fairness</p><p>Money doesn’t buy happiness, we’re told. But they will try every trick in the book to hang on to their stash and woe betide the tax authority that tries to lay a finger on their treasure.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/27/democracy-tax-billionaires">Continue reading...</a></description>

<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comMon, 02 Nov 2026 22:24:02 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Lenders owed combined €11m want to cross-examine Paddy McKillen jnr]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/02/legal-costs-order-made-against-mckillen-jnr-after-failed-bid-to-set-aside-bankruptcy-summons/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/02/legal-costs-order-made-against-mckillen-jnr-after-failed-bid-to-set-aside-bankruptcy-summons/Mon, 02 Nov 2026 20:07:15 +0000Lenders owed a combined €11 million by Paddy McKillen jnr want to cross-examine the businessman under oath on his financial affairs, the High Court has heard.

Lawyers for McKillen are opposing the examination, submitting that it is an attempt to embarrass him.

McKillen is seeking a personal insolvency arrangement, and has told the court he has debts of €27.7 million and is insolvent. In September, the court granted him a protective certificate, which protects him from his creditors until at least December.

Lenders Herbert Street Finance and Cabriz Finance – who are owed €2.3 million and €8.7 million, respectively, by McKillen – have both issued applications to set aside the protective certificate.

The applications arise from concerns raised by the lenders about an alleged “absence of detail” in information provided by McKillen in his application for a protective certificate.

In written evidence filed last week, McKillen rejected allegations that he had failed to disclose certain financial information when he was granted a protective certificate.

Bernard Dunleavy, counsel for Herbert Street Finance, told Judge Nessa Cahill on Monday his side was seeking to examine McKillen in relation to his assets and liabilities.

Dunleavy, appearing with barrister Niall Ó hUiginn, submitted that, per recent evidence sworn by insolvency practitioner Eugene McDarby, a revised statement of McKillen’s financial affairs will be required.

According to an affidavit sworn by McDarby, a judgment against McKillen – obtained by Herbert Street Finance in October for a debt of €2.3 million – as well as “other developments, including information provided by creditors during the protective certificate period”, gave rise to the need for an updated prescribed financial statement.

Dunleavy said that whatever information is gleaned from the examination will be for the benefit of all of McKillen’s creditors.

Keith Farry, barrister for McKillen, said his side was not consenting to the examination, and submitted the application was “a show for embarrassing Mr McKillen in front of the court”.

Dunleavy said his client was “not in the business of embarrassing anyone”.

The judge made directions for the filing of written submissions on the question of McKillen’s examination, and adjourned the case for two weeks.

Separately, McKillen has been ordered by the court to pay legal costs incurred by Herbert Street Finance in opposing the businessman’s bid to strike down a bankruptcy summons over a debt exceeding €2 million.

Herbert Street Finance in January issued the bankruptcy summons, the first step in bankruptcy proceedings, over the debt it said McKillen owed it.

In August, Judge Liam Kennedy dismissed an application by McKillen to set aside the summons.

At a hearing on Monday, Ó hUiginn, for Herbert Street Finance, told Kennedy he was seeking an order for his client’s legal costs, following its successful defence of the set-aside application.

Ó hUiginn noted that if the court made the costs order sought, it would be captured by the protective certificate granted to McKillen.

Farry said he could not consent to the costs order sought, but said his side recognised the lender had been successful in opposing the set-aside application.

The judge awarded the costs of the set-aside application to Herbert Street Finance.

The substantive bankruptcy petition was adjourned to January.

McKillen is the co-founder of the hospitality group Press Up.

]]>Collins Photos<![CDATA[New EU charge to push up prices for many online shoppers]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/02/new-eu-charge-set-to-see-prices-spike-for-many-online-shoppers/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/02/new-eu-charge-set-to-see-prices-spike-for-many-online-shoppers/Mon, 02 Nov 2026 15:57:29 +0000Parcels arriving in Ireland from outside of the European Union will be hit with charges of at least €5 per item as a result of two distinct fees that are now applied.

The new €2 “Union Handling Fee” that came into effect on Sunday is on top of a €3 customs charge per item that was introduced earlier this year.

The charges and fees are mandated at EU level, with delivery companies given the legal responsibility to collect them if the levies have not been paid during online checkout.

The new charge is intended to cover the increased costs incurred by customs authorities due to the huge growth of ecommerce in recent years. It will apply to all goods, regardless of their value, once a seller ships them to Ireland from outside the EU.

The growth in online marketplaces – based in China primarily – has caused dramatic upheaval in retail. According to official estimates, about six billion packages with a value of less than €150 came into EU states from outside the bloc last year.

New charges mean online shopping is now a lot more expensive

As of now, when a package valued at €10 containing a pen, notebook and keyring is bought from outside the EU, it will attract a customs duty charge of €9, comprising three lots of €3.

The EU handling fee of €2 per item adds a further €6 to the bill, bringing the total end cost to €25.

Consumers will be expected to pay the charges in one of two ways.

Some larger ecommerce operations will be set up to collect the customs duty and EU handling fee at the point of sale.

In such circumstances, both charges will be shown to the consumer and the total price paid at the checkout will be the final price, with no extra charges on delivery.

Other websites may not collect these charges at checkout and the delivery company will be required to collect the money from the consumer.

When charges have to be collected in this way it is likely a further administrative fee of about €7 will be added to the total by the delivery company.

In such cases, the three small items that had an initial price tag totalling €10 could end up costing Irish consumers €32, or more than three times the original value.

There is no customs duty or EU handling fee if goods are based in Ireland, Northern Ireland or in another EU member state at the time they are ordered.

]]>ronstik<![CDATA[Energy shares fall on Strait of Hormuz signals as European banking proves to be safe bet]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/02/energy-shares-fall-on-strait-of-hormuz-signals-as-european-banking-proves-to-be-safe-bet/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/02/energy-shares-fall-on-strait-of-hormuz-signals-as-european-banking-proves-to-be-safe-bet/Mon, 02 Nov 2026 19:54:06 +0000Global stocks held steady on Monday, although international energy companies were rattled by falling oil prices prompted by US president Donald Trump signalling a potential deal with Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Shares in the banking sector proved to be a safe bet across Europe, with leading national banks boosting local stock indices. Closer to home, Ryanair’s share price soared following the publication of the airline’s financial results.

Dublin

The Iseq All-Share index increase 1.49 per cent to close at 14,417.86 on Monday, with Ryanair leading the charge into the green and only two listed companies falling in share price.

Ryanair was up 5.24 per cent to close at €24.10 a share following the publication of its financial results. Despite a 15 per cent fall in profits, which amounted to €2.15 billion, the airline’s chief executive Michael O’Leary committed to the company expanding, although perhaps with a boost from higher air fares.

The financial services sector held steady, with Bank of Ireland seeing its share price rise 1.20 per cent to €18.58 a share and AIB up 0.23 per cent to €10.93. PTSB saw no change in its share price of €2.95, following a week of High Court proceedings of its proposed sale to Austrian lender Bawag.

London

The London Stock Exchange began the trading week just about in the green, with strong returns from well known retail brands bringing the city’s top indices higher. The blue-chip FTSE 100 closed 0.29 higher at close of markets, while the more domestically-minded mid-cap FTSE 250 was up 1.40 per cent.

C&C, the drinks giant with Bulmers cider and Five Lamps beer under its portfolio, saw its share prices increase 4.26 per cent following a drop off last week after the company revealed a three per cent decrease in net profit last year.

Lloyds and Barclays banks also began the week in the green, with their share prices up 1.84 per cent and 2.18 per cent, respectively. Meanwhile, British oil and gas giant BP dropped 4.37 per cent, as crude oil prices dropped sharply in the aftermath of comments made by Trump on an agreement with Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Europe

Shares across the Continent grew moderately, boosted by large gains in the banking industry that drew back losses in the energy sector. The blue-chip Stoxx 50 Index rose 0.74 per and the mid-market Stoxx 600 Index by 0.45 at close of markets.

Spain’s Santander Bank saw its share price increase 2.65 per cent, as it returns to stability following falls last week prompted by the Brazilian presidential election. German rival Deutsche Bank, meanwhile, was up 1.70 per cent and France’s BNP Paribas followed along, rising 1.62 per cent by close.

But losses in the energy sector drew Europe’s leading indices down in overall share prices. Italian oil and gas company Eni Spa saw its share price fall 2.84 per cent and France’s Total Energies by 2.47 per cent at end of trading hours, in a similar fate to their British rival bp

New York

Early trades on Wall Street had a strong start to the week thanks to renewed confidence in more traditional stocks, with investors holding their nerves as the US prepares to vote in midterm elections to elect their next congressional class.

The Nasdaq 100 index rose nearly 0.50 per cent, while the S&P 500 jumped some 0.60 per cent and the Dow Jones Industrial Average increased nearly one per cent before midday New York Time.

Shipping and ecommerce giant Amazon saw its share price rise over four per cent following an upgrade in its price target and recommendations from leading analysts, while electric vehicle manufacturer Tesla was up some 2.5 per cent.

Apple’s stock, however, fell 1.30 per cent in the morning as investors retreated from trading in advance of the technology company’s earning report being released.

]]>Artem_Egorov<![CDATA[Magnum sues Aldi for trademark infringement over ‘Gianni’ ice creams]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/02/magnum-sues-aldi-for-trademark-infringement-over-gianni-ice-creams/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/02/magnum-sues-aldi-for-trademark-infringement-over-gianni-ice-creams/Mon, 02 Nov 2026 17:45:36 +0000The Magnum Ice Cream Company, which makes several well-known brands of ice cream, is suing Aldi in Ireland for alleged trademark infringement.

It is claimed Aldi’s “Gianni” range of ice creams are copycat products sold in a form or style of packaging which is identical or confusingly similar to a number of Magnum products.

The Magnum Group, which is headquartered in Amsterdam, says it is the world’s largest ice cream company with revenues of €7.9 billion and is home to the world’s five largest ice cream brands, which include Magnum, Ben and Jerry’s and Cornetto.

By 2025, it had 21 per cent of the global ice cream market, 16,500 employees, 30 factories, 12 research and development centres, and about three million freezer cabinets. It was formerly part of the Unilever group.

On Monday, Judge Eileen Roberts admitted to the Commercial Court proceedings brought by the Magnum Ice Cream Company NV, Magnum IP Holdings BV, Magnum ICC Europe BV and Magnum ICC Ireland Ltd against Aldi Stores (Ireland) Ltd alleging “passing off” and breach of trademark.

Magnum global intellectual property (IP) media and marketing general counsel Katherine Tsang said in an affidavit seeking entry of the case to the commercial list that she became aware, following a review started late last year, of a line of copycat ice cream or ice lolly products being sold in Aldi supermarkets in the UK and Ireland.

Following investigation, she said, it became apparent the defendant was selling copycat versions of Magnum, Vienetta, Feast, Ben and Jerry’s, Solero, Twister and Cornetto products.

She said while many of these have been on the market for some years, the defendant has continually and in synchronisation modified its brands and packaging so as to look increasingly like the products in the Magnum range.

On September 24th last, Magnum’s lawyers issued a “cease and desist” letter to Aldi but as of October 15th, Tsang said, no substantive response had been received from Aldi’s solicitors.

Following an application to have the case entered into the fast track commercial list from Glen Gibbons, counsel for Magnum, the judge approved agreed directions for the hearing of the case and adjourned it to next April.

]]>Andy Rain<![CDATA[State’s wealth fund commits €100m to Dublin ‘smart office’ development]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/02/states-wealth-fund-commits-100-million-to-dublin-smart-office-development/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/02/states-wealth-fund-commits-100-million-to-dublin-smart-office-development/Mon, 02 Nov 2026 14:26:39 +0000An investment of €100 million has been committed by the State’s sovereign wealth fund towards the construction of an ultra-modern “smart office” block in Dublin’s south inner city, the commercial property developer behind the project has said.

This will act as the starting point for IPUT Real Estate’s €500 million premium office development pipeline, the company added, and “marks a deepening of the relationship” between the firm and the Ireland Strategic Investment Fund (ISIF), a development fund under the directorship of the National Treasury Management Agency.

The money is earmarked for the development of 29 Earlsfort Terrace, the former office of Deloitte Ireland. IPUT bought the building in 2018 as part of a series of transactions that included two other central Dublin properties, for a combined €160 million.

The site sits at the corner of Hatch Street and Earlsfort Terrace, equidistant to the Grand Canal and St Stephen’s Green in Dublin 2. Across the road from the National Concert Hall, its neighbours include the headquarters of law firms Arthur Cox and Eversheds Sutherland and investment bank KKR.
