Investors are often advised to let their profits run, but banking gains feels good. It may also make us feel clever – even if we’re anything but.

A forthcoming Journal of Finance paper, Disposed to Be Overconfident, suggests profit-taking can distort our memories and judgment.

When judging their stock-picking abilities, ordinary investors rarely bother with overall portfolio returns or comparisons with the market. Instead, the study says, they use a simpler scorecard: how many stocks they sold at a profit versus how many sold at a loss.

By selling winners quickly, holding on to losers, and remembering the former more fondly, investors convince themselves they are better stock-pickers than their overall returns suggest.

The researchers found evidence of how skewed this scorecard can be. Ordinary Dutch investors recalled selling an average of 4.22 stocks at a profit over a year, almost twice the 2.17 recorded in their trading histories.

In a subsequent experiment, traders who were forced to sell winning stocks became more confident of their abilities than those forced to sell losers. And yet, the two groups picked virtually the same number of winning stocks and made almost identical overall profits. Simply realising a profit made people feel more skilful than they really were.

Fake news: why investors keep believing stories they know are false

The researchers link this to the disposition effect, the tendency to sell winners too early while hanging on to losers. The resulting scorecard is flattering, with profits banked and remembered, while losses remain unrealised and out of sight.

However, it can drive a vicious cycle: profit-taking builds overconfidence, which encourages over-trading, which degrades wealth through bad timing and transaction fees.

Our pleasure in hearing the cash register ring is natural. However, the sound of money being banked doesn’t mean we know what we’re doing.

AI is the next test of that success. Ireland is already one of Europe’s leading adopters of AI, but the question now is how we use that position to build AI businesses, to develop intellectual property and to create lasting economic value in Ireland.

Ireland has spent decades building an enviable position at the intersection of US technology investment and the European single market. Ambition is everything and Ireland should now aim not only to host, regulate and use AI, but also to become a place where valuable AI products are developed and commercialised.

There is a strong foundation from which to do so. Microsoft’s latest Global AI Diffusion report puts Ireland’s AI user share at 49.9 per cent, the highest in the EU and significantly above the global average of 18.8 per cent. It gives Ireland a strong starting point.

Much of the global debate about AI has focused on the foundations of the technology: energy, chips, data centres and large AI models. Those layers do matter and Ireland already has significant assets in technology infrastructure.

For Ireland, however, the greatest opportunity may lie higher up the value chain in the application layer, the applications that turn AI capability into useful products and services for particular industries.

Where Ireland Can Compete

Ireland already has considerable expertise in sectors where AI could change how complex businesses operate, including technology, financial services, life sciences and healthcare. Businesses here do not need to build the next frontier model to create valuable AI intellectual property. They can combine their knowledge of those industries with increasingly capable AI tools to develop products that their clients will actually use and which can solve real commercial problems.

The investment environment is also encouraging.

The challenge is to ensure that this activity translates into businesses, intellectual property, specialist employment and economic value that remain in Ireland. None of this will be straightforward.

Energy and infrastructure pressures cannot be ignored, competition for skilled people is intense and other European countries are pursuing the same investment.

Regulatory complexity can also affect where new products are tested and commercialised. That makes it all the more important that Ireland focuses on areas where its existing strengths give it an advantage, rather than trying to replicate the scale of AI infrastructure being developed elsewhere.

Getting Regulation Right

Regulation is part of that picture. Ireland should not have to choose between having effective regulation or having a competitive AI sector. ]]><![CDATA[Can you really ‘make your money back’ on UK pension in two years and eight months?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/01/can-you-really-make-your-money-back-on-uk-pension-in-two-years-and-eight-months/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/01/can-you-really-make-your-money-back-on-uk-pension-in-two-years-and-eight-months/Sun, 01 Nov 2026 11:22:44 +0000I’m still confused about a UK pensions article you wrote some time back. The person had 20 years of contributions and it takes 35 years to get a full pension, so a difference of 15 years.

Are you saying that if she now pays Class 3 contributions of £956.80 for the next 15 years (costing her not too far off £15k), she will have that £15k back after drawing the pension for two years and eight months?

R O’N

It all seems a bit fantastic but, in pure maths terms, that is exactly how it works. However, there are a couple of “real world” issues you need to take into account that will skew that simplicity.

We will come to that in a bit, but first let’s crunch the numbers.

Hundreds of thousands of Irish people – possibly millions – have spent time working in the UK at some point in their careers before returning home or moving on elsewhere. The fact that they could be entitled to a weekly UK state pension – currently paid at £241.30 (€288.50) a week – could make a big difference to some of them.

In 2026/27 – the current UK tax year – it will cost you £18.40 a week to buy back Class 3 national insurance contributions to boost your UK pension. That comes to £956.80 (€1,145.50) a year.

Regular readers will be aware that the cheaper Class 2 contributions many paid to buy back up to 18 years over cover recently are no longer available to people paying voluntary national insurance from abroad. So Class 3 is where we are at from now on.

The current full UK state pension is, as I said, £241.30 and each year you buy back will add £6.89 per week – one thirty-fifth of 241.30 – to the pension you eventually receive at today’s prices. That amounts to £358.28 extra in pension over the course of a year.

Pensions: The most important step is simply getting started

To find out how long it will take you to “make back” what you have paid in, you simple divide the £956.80 cost by the extra pension you get on the back of it – £358.28. That gives you a figure of 2.67 per cent, or just a shade over two years and eight months.

For someone buying back 15 years, the same holds true: you are simply multiplying both the contributions and the benefit by a factor of 15 so you are not changing the math.

But now we come to where reality intrudes into the basic math.

The contributions you are paying come from already taxed income. As in Ireland national insurance is a form of tax, with a small “t”. But the money you receive in retirement will likely be liable for income tax and USC in Ireland, assuming you live here.

If you are paying income tax at 20 per cent, the extra pension amount into your hand each year for every additional year’s contribution you make drops to £286.62. On that basis it would take you 3.35 years, three years and about four months, to make back what you paid in.

If you pay tax at 40 per cent, the benefit in your pocket falls to £214.97 a year for each year’s additional contribution. On that basis, you would not be in “profit” on the arrangement until 4.45 years after you draw down the pension – close to 4½ years.

How to navigate and maximise Ireland’s State pension

USC will extend that again but, given the multiple rates, I’m not going into that in detail. Suffice to say that it will extend the “pay back” period slightly.

However, on average, an Irish man can expect to live for 15 years in retirement and a woman almost 19, so it still seems like a good idea.

There are a couple of other issues that clearly affect the precise payback time.

One is that you are dealing with currency risk. There is no way of putting a figure on this but, clearly, the euro/sterling exchange rates when you make the payment and when you eventually draw down the pension will be different. Whether that benefits you or penalises you, only time can tell.

Then you need to remember that both the pension payable and the cost of these Class 3 contributions tend to change each year. For instance, the full UK pension rate will rise to £250.70 a week.

You do also need to bear in mind that the British are once again fiddling with how they work out pension increases – largely because the current “triple lock” is proving expensive in the context of other demands on exchequer funds.

Your pension: how to make up for lost time

As of now, the tiple locks guarantees that the state pension will rise by the highest of inflation, average earnings growth or 2.5 per cent. From April 2030, unless things change again between now and then, the link to earnings is gone – leaving pension increases to rise by 2.5 per cent or the rate of inflation, whichever is higher.

The expectation, certainly in Whitehall, is that this will reduce the scale of annual pension increases.

That all makes it difficult to be absolutely definitive on these things but, given that the UK state pension this woman receives in 15 years time (or whenever she subsequently retires) will be higher than it is today, it will in fact take less than the time given above to recover her outlay.

Of course, that does have to be offset against the “opportunity cost” – what return that money might have delivered if invested other than in buying back UK pension years – but we’re definitely not getting into that here.

There is one other issue that might skew the numbers. The 35-year timeline for people to secure a full UK state pension is based on someone who starts paying national insurance in 2016 when the new system came into force.

Of course, for the majority of Irish – and others – who are considering voluntary contributions, their UK national insurance record will have started earlier, many decades earlier in some cases. Under the old system, as I understand it, people could secure a full basic state pension on the back of 30 years contribution – but those who retired on this pension before 2016 receive a lower weekly payment.

So they really need to get a fix on what their UK pension position is.

According to the UK government website, they will work out your starting (2016) position under the new state pension. You will be entitled to the higher of the amount you would have got under the old system or the amount you would qualify for under the new system if it had been in place when you started making contributions.

This is important because you then know how many years of contributions you need to make on a voluntary basis to qualify for the maximum pension. It might not be as straightforward as “I worked there for 20 years, so I need another 15 years of voluntary contributions”... or it might.

Confusing? Yep, but that’s what happens when a country changes the way it calculates pension rights.

Anyway, to get a definitive answer, you can check your current pension situation with the UK authorities. There is a user-friendly online system but it does require a UK government ID which many who once worked in the UK will not have.

The alternatives are to contract them via a dedicated email form they provide, though they do warn that it is taking some time to reply to emails.

You can also try phoning – at +44 (0)191 2187777 – though regular readers will be aware of my view that confirmation in writing is always a good idea. Or you can write to them at: The Pension Service 11, Mail Handling Site A, Wolverhampton, WV98 1LW, England.

When Kerry-born Gráinne Walsh went to Seville to study at the Universidad de Sevilla on an Erasmus programme in 1996, she found love in the form of a local man, Alfonso. Walsh’s first spell in Seville was part of a wider international business and languages degree at DCU. She fell in love with the city straight away.

“I came in mid-September and loved the blue skies and warm weather. A bottle of decent wine cost 350 pesetas (about €2). You could go out at 11pm when you would be coming home from the pub at home.”

Walsh returned to Dublin to finish her degree, but Alfonso soon followed to ask for her hand in marriage.

“I was only 20 at the time; he was 27. I let my heart rule my head. I said yes, but on one condition. I needed to travel before I settled down. A Wicklow woman in Marbella: ‘I would make friends in the summer and they would then go home. But I found my tribe’

Walsh was keen to secure a professional role in Seville so she researched companies with Irish links. She found a marketing position at a local brewer, Cruzcampo, then a subsidiary of Guinness, and later purchased by Heineken.

“My name Gráinne was unpronounceable. They ended up calling me Walsh. I went on to positions in HR and corporate relations. I had the best job in the house and enjoyed every day.

“Cruzcampo is an institution locally, a company where people stay for life and I spent almost 20 years there. Working there was a great experience for me but, by 2017, I had a hankering to do something else.”

Walsh undertook a master’s in coaching and, by 2019, felt confident to strike out on her own. Covid soon struck, but she was able to secure coaching business online and also found a part-time academic position as an associate professor at Universidad Loyola, where she lectures on business degree programmes.

Today, her work also involves leadership training programmes for corporates. A core part of her work involves teaching participants soft skills such as assertiveness, empathy and emotional intelligence. Among her multinational clients is Navantia, the owners of Harland & Wolff shipbuilders, and her work takes her to Britain and Ireland as well as the rest of Spain.

Walsh says the workplace culture in Spain has traditionally been very macho and less progressive than in Ireland but this is beginning to change.

“Spanish women have faced significant challenges. In the corporate world, they have been trying to juggle balls, being the perfect professional while also being a good wife and mother. Fortunately, thanks to Covid, there’s more acceptance of remote working and work-life balance and things are starting to improve.”

From Navan to Valencia: ‘They refer to the Irish here as the Latins of the north’

Life in Seville is good, and Walsh says it has been a safe city to raise their children who are aged 16-22. She loves its traditions, especially around holy week at Easter and says April is a beautiful time to visit when Seville’s famous orange trees blossom.

“For me it’s a perfect-sized city. Its big but not too big. You can walk around it safely. It’s small enough to be spontaneous. You can say to someone that you will meet them in 15 minutes.

“The tourist boom, though, means that locals now have to do the unthinkable and make reservations in their favourite restaurants.”

The significant increase in tourism in recent years has also been accompanied with concern about rising property prices, with locals often priced out of the market. Mirroring other parts of Spain, this has added fuel to the social unrest as a result of big cost of living increases in recent years.

“Inflation has definitely hit in, but it is still a lot cheaper than Ireland. You can still buy a coffee for €1.80.”

The family live in a town house on the edge of the city centre, featuring the essential ingredients of air conditioning and a pool in the back garden to escape Seville’s hot summers. Weekends are often spent down at the coast in Huelva.

People in Seville are either Huelva beachgoers or Cadiz beach goers, she says. While they are both on the Atlantic, Huelva has a more relaxed family vibe, while Cadiz attracts young surfers and those seeking a livelier night scene.

“Social life is outdoors 10 months of the year. We like to sail and we have a boat in Huelva, which is our floating house.”

Walsh misses the easy hospitable and warm personality of the Irish but has no intention of returning home.

“I do miss the green fields of Ireland. We did an extended house exchange with my parents when the kids were very young and spent some time in Cahersiveen.

“I worried about what would happen if I fell in love with the Irish lifestyle. Two weeks into the grey skies and pouring rain of south Kerry, that decision about where we would live became a lot easier.”

]]><![CDATA[Audi looks west amid slump in Chinese demand ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/31/audi-looks-west-amid-slump-in-chinese-demand/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/31/audi-looks-west-amid-slump-in-chinese-demand/Sun, 01 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000Audi’s ahead-through-engineering days are long behind it, at least to judge by the bumpy week just gone.

On Friday, the VW subsidiary slashed its earnings forecast by 87 per cent in the third quarter, blaming the ongoing decline in its Chinese market meltdown paired with chafing Chinese inroads into Europe.

With Audi’s foreign sales down by a fifth, a little creative accounting secured a tiny Q3 profit of €87 million and kept the Ingolstadt luxury car brand out of the red for another three months.

German union IG Metall wins right to 28-hour working week and 4.3% pay rise

It is Audi’s second such forecast cut this year, with maximum revenues of €59 billion now likely, down €4 billion from its previous forecast.

For Audi chief financial officer Jürgen Rittersberger, the message of the dire numbers was clear: “Enormous pressure to act at Audi will wait for no one.”

He was echoing chief financial officer Arno Antlitz a day earlier at Audi’s VW parent, as he revealed a €5.86 billion third-quarter loss at the firm as it looks to find €31 billion in cost savings.

At an Audi board meeting on Friday, managers were said to be praying for miracles from their US chief executive Gernot Döllner. The 57-year-old became a household name in Germany this week after a high-profile election campaign appearance alongside US president Donald Trump in Georgia.

Döllner was there to announce Audi’s first plant in the southern US state: a €4 billion investment promising 4,500 new jobs to produce up to 200,000 SUVs annually from 2030. Reportedly the largest such investment in Georgia’s history, Trump was quick to take credit for the “incredible” investment and linked it all to his administration’s tariff regime.

Those tariffs will be eased, according to the Wall Street Journal on Friday, for car companies like Audi that commit to manufacturing in the US.

Germany’s powerful IG Metall trade union denounced Döllner’s appearance as a “flagrant breach of his own company’s rules, which expressly require political neutrality in the run-up to elections”.

Döllner had “allowed himself to be turned into a puppet in the propaganda show” of Trump, according to the union.

The US subsidiary insisted the appearance had been cleared with Ingolstadt beforehand and that it “accepted this invitation solely with Audi’s best interests in mind”.

Given the looming corporate cliff edge, it looks like Audi has decided to go for broke – figuratively, of course.

]]>BRENDAN SMIALOWSKI

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3446868/">

   <description>Auch in Österreich sind nun Fälle von Nägeln in Halloween-Zuckerln publik geworden: Im Linzer Stadtteil Oed entdeckte ein Vater gleich in mehreren Süßigkeiten seiner Kinder Nägel.    <title>Kühlsysteme in Supermärkten gehackt</title>
   <description>Supermärkte in mehreren europäischen Ländern sind in der Nacht auf Montag Ziel von Cyberangriffen auf ihre Kühl- und Gefriersysteme geworden. Poland’s ambassador to the United Nations, Krzysztof Szczerski, has resigned, becoming the third Polish ambassador to do so since a government-backed move by a group of judges to take control of the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) in Warsaw.

All three of the departing ambassadors were previously aides or advisers to former President Andrzej Duda, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party. They have criticised the attempt to oust the TK’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, who was appointed to the court under PiS.

Following the resignations of Poland’s Ambassadors to China and Romania, Prof. Krzysztof Szczerski, Poland’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations, has also submitted his resignation.

All three are senior state officials and experienced diplomats who have served at the…

— Marcin Przydacz (@marcin_przydacz) November 2, 2026

On Monday afternoon, foreign ministry spokesman Maciej Wewiór announced that Szczerski had “submitted a request to shorten his diplomatic mission at the UN”, where he has served as ambassador since 2021.

Szczerski’s resignation followed those of Jakub Kumoch, Poland’s ambassador to China, and Paweł Soloch, the Polish envoy to Romania, who quit their posts on Friday and Saturday, respectively.

While Szczerski has not yet commented on the reasons for his departure, Kumoch and Soloch made clear that their decisions were motivated by Friday’s move to suspend Święczkowski from the TK.

Soloch wrote that the “attempt to unlawfully take over the Constitutional Tribunal” left him with “no possibility of continuing to serve as ambassador”. Kumoch said his decision was a “matter of conscience”, as “there are certain things I cannot explain abroad without losing face, and I have no intention of speaking ill of Poland”.

There is chaos at Poland's constitutional court tonight as a group of government-backed judges moved to take control from the opposition-aligned chief justice.

Riot police have surrounded the court and were seen preventing the chief justice from entering https://t.co/xpkp3sjPFn

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 30, 2026

Szczerski previously served as a member of the European Parliament for PIS. In 2015, he joined the chancellery of PiS-aligned President Duda, later becoming the head of his cabinet and then head of his International Policy Bureau.

Kumoch was a member of Duda’s National Development Council, an advisory body to the president, before serving as ambassador to Switzerland, Turkey, and then China. Soloch was the head of Duda’s National Security Bureau from 2015 to 2022.

On Monday, after Szczerski’s resignation, foreign minister Radosław Sikorski suggested that the three ambassadors had quit at the urging of the current president, Karol Nawrocki, who is also aligned with PiS.

Sikorski sardonically suggested that, in contrast to Polish ambassadors who quit in 1981 over the imposition of martial law despite “risking vengeance from the communist regime”, the newly resigned trio “will surely be handsomely rewarded for their heroic deeds”.

 

The developments are part of a much broader fallout from the crisis around the TK, which began on Friday evening when large numbers of riot police appeared outside the court.

It soon transpired that a group of eight judges appointed by parliament to the TK this year – but five of whom Nawrocki has refused to swear in – had entered the court and declared that Święczkowski had been suspended from his position for failing to fulfil his duties.

Święczkowski, who before becoming a TK judge previously served as a member of the former PiS government, declared their actions unlawful and an attempted “coup d’état”. He has been backed by the six other justices appointed when PiS was in government.

Święczkowski has also been supported by Nawrocki, who dramatically entered the court in the early hours of Saturday morning, clashing physically and verbally with the self-proclaimed acting head of the court, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska.

During a visit to the Constitutional Tribunal last night, President Nawrocki clashed physically and verbally with judges involved in an attempt to take control of the court.

The president is today seeking talks with political leaders to discuss the crisis https://t.co/7HmBnuIaDG

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 31, 2026

The developments have created an unprecedented situation at the TK. However, the court has been in crisis since 2015, when Duda and the then-PiS government – which came to power that year – unlawfully rejected three judges appointed by the former parliament and replaced them with three of their own.

Poland’s first-ever nest of Asian hornets, an invasive species seen as a particular threat because it preys on honeybees, has been eliminated. But scientists who have studied the colony say that it is likely more will be found next year.

Since arriving in France in 2004, Asian hornets, which are indigenous to Southeast Asia, have gradually spread to other European countries.

The first confirmed nest to be found in Poland was sighted in a tree in the village of Wielka Wieś near Kraków in mid-October, with individual hornets also being spotted at the apiary of the city’s AGH University of Science and Technology.

The nest was removed last week and sent to be studied by a team of scientists at Wrocław University of Environmental and Life Sciences, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP).

Paweł Migdał, from the university’s faculty of biology and animal science, told PAP that the nest was “fairly large” considering the Polish climate, containing around 1,000 workers and several dozen queens and males.

The scientists’ assessment of the nest revealed that it contained eggs and larvae, indicating that the hornets inhabiting it were still feeding, he added.

“I think we’ll find more of these nests,” Migdał told PAP. “They’re often built in the treetops, which means they’re invisible until the leaves fall in the autumn.”

Young queens had already left the nest to establish new ones after overwintering, and have greater chances of surviving the longer and warmer the Polish autumn is, he explained. They seek shelter in warm, dry places, such as underground or in storage areas.

 

With queens measuring 30mm and males about 24mm, Asian hornets, also known as the yellow-legged hornet, are smaller than the European variety, and no more dangerous to humans than European hornets or wasps.

The major concern over their arrival relates to their tendency to seek out beehives and prey on honeybees.

“Besides killing honeybees, their presence also causes bees in apiaries to stop working,” explained Migdał. “With the European hornet, the bees recognise the threat but, in a sense, continue working. However, the yellow-legged hornet presents a completely new threat to them.”

The number of bee colonies in Poland has risen 54% over the last decade to reach two million, thanks in part to a state programme supporting beekeepers.

Bees' value to the ecosystem as pollinators is estimated to be worth 5bn zloty (€1.1bn) https://t.co/ElISOc2o2T

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 30, 2022

The scale of the species’ invasiveness is shown by the fact that it releases an average of 150 young queens from its nest, and sometimes even 500 – each of which can potentially create its own nest – while European hornets release just 50, Migdał pointed out.

The location of the first nest found in Poland surprised scientists as the closest previously known was in Opava, around 150 km away in the Czech Republic. The hornets therefore probably travelled in a vehicle, although Migdał noted a potential concern that other populations might be found between the two sites.

The creation of accelerated renewable energy development zones stems from the EU’s revised Renewable Energy Directive (RED III), which requires member states to designate areas where renewable energy projects can be developed more quickly.

The Church Fund, originally established in 1950 to compensate religious communities for property seized by the communist authorities, provides state subsidies for the health insurance contributions of clergy, for religious organisations’ charitable activities, and for the renovation of religious buildings.

Most of this money is then used to cover 80% of clergy members’ social security contributions. Under the bill proposed by The Left, churches would pay half of the contributions, with clergy covering the other half.

A Turkish software engineer has, with the help of AI and vast quantities of Polish public data, created a precise digital replica of Warsaw, the city where he lives.

The map, which can be explored for free online, features almost 200,000 buildings, moving trams that match their real-life schedules, changing light and weather conditions, and over 45,000 accurately placed streetlamps that turn on at night. It is even possible to fly a virtual plane through the city.

The person behind the project, Bedirhan Yildirim, was inspired by recent efforts to produce similar maps of New York and London.

While he initially considered producing one of Istanbul, his hometown, he decided instead to pick the city he lives in, Warsaw. “It is smaller, mostly flat, and I walk its streets every day,” he explained of his choice.

Yildirim then used AI coding agents to create the map through a process of trial and error, constantly tweaking and improving the model.

The initial version took only two days to produce and was launched on 22 October, but it has been regularly improved since then based on feedback from users.

 

The work was made possible by what Yildirim says is the “incredible amount of data” Poland’s national mapping office, GUGiK, provides for free, including 3D building models, terrain scans, and even details of almost 2 million trees.

Further information, including on parks, streetlamps, and traffic lights, was taken from OpenStreetMap, a freely licensed database. Meanwhile, timetables from Warsaw’s public transport authority, ZTM, and Poland’s national rail operator, PKP, allowed the map to feature accurately timed trams and trains.

Current weather conditions are input from Open-Meteo, an open-source meteorological service. But users can also choose to manually adjust the time of day or year, with light and weather changing accordingly.

This week’s agreement builds upon the Northolt Treaty signed by Poland and the UK in May this year, under which the two countries agreed to cooperate more closely on security.

Last year, Poland signed a similar agreement upgrading relations with France. That followed a strategic partnership agreement with Sweden the previous year.

In April this year, Poland signed new comprehensive strategic partnership agreements with South Korea and Japan. This year, it has also deepened security ties with Canada and Norway.

In November, Poland will host the first military exercises organised by the so-called Coalition of the Willing. Thousands of personnel from the UK, Poland, France and Germany will test operational readiness for a multinational force to secure a potential future Ukraine peace deal.

City AM https://www.cityam.com/ London's Business Newspaper Mon, 02 Nov 2026 18:47:12 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.4 https://www.cityam.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/app_launcher_icon_final_rounded.png?w=32 City AM https://www.cityam.com/ 32 32 213406410 Anthropic’s growth slows ahead of IPO as AI spending bill nears $900bn https://www.cityam.com/anthropics-growth-slows-ahead-of-ipo-as-ai-spending-bill-nears-900bn/ Mon, 02 Nov 2026 18:47:02 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2473830

Anthropic’s revenue has surged twelvefold to nearly $17bn (£13bn), but the AI giant has slipped back into the red as its computing commitments approach $900bn ahead of a potentially record-breaking stock market debut. The Claude maker revealed the figures in an updated IPO filing on Monday, offering investors a fresh look at its finances just [...]]]>

Anthropic’s revenue has surged twelvefold to nearly $17bn (£13bn), but the AI giant has slipped back into the red as its computing commitments approach $900bn ahead of a potentially record-breaking stock market debut.

The Claude maker revealed the figures in an updated IPO filing on Monday, offering investors a fresh look at its finances just weeks before its expected Nasdaq listing.

Revenue jumped from $1.4bn a year earlier to almost $17bn in the three months to September, although quarterly growth slowed sharply to 47 per cent, compared with 144 per cent in the previous quarter.

The slowdown comes as Anthropic faces growing competition from cheaper AI models and mounting pressure to justify the extraordinary sums being spent on computing infrastructure.

The company reported a $567m operating loss for the quarter, reversing a $974m profit in the previous three months, its first profitable quarter.

Operating expenses climbed 292 per cent year on year to $17.5bn, including $5bn in short-term computing costs after demand exceeded the capacity secured under its existing agreements.

Anthropic’s $900bn computing bill

The updated prospectus revealed that Anthropic has committed approximately $895bn to future spending, almost entirely on computing infrastructure and data centres.

Around $448bn is due by the end of 2030, including roughly $70bn over the next 12 months.

The commitments are almost seven times the firm’s $132bn cash and short-term investment pile, raising concerns about how quickly revenue can catch up with its infrastructure costs.

Its largest agreements include $161bn in equipment leases with Broadcom, $121bn with Google and up to $120.5bn with SpaceX’s AI business.

Meanwhile, price cuts on newer models and discounts offered to customers knocked around $600m off third-quarter revenue.

Anthropic also disclosed that between five and seven per cent of revenue in the first nine months of the year came from customers violating its usage policies or commercial terms, warning that tougher enforcement could weigh on future growth.

Record IPO on the horizon

Anthropic reported a $23.3bn net loss for the quarter, bringing its losses for the first nine months of 2026 to $104bn.

However, the vast majority reflects non-cash accounting adjustments linked to convertible notes and other securities, whose value has risen alongside the company’s valuation.

Revenue for the nine-month period reached $33.2bn, up roughly 1,200 per cent from a year earlier.

Anthropic is preparing to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, potentially before the US Thanksgiving holiday later this month.

Investors have reportedly discussed a valuation of between $1.4 trillion and $1.5 trillion, although a figure closer to $1.75 trillion could be achievable, according to Bloomberg analysts.

The offering could rival SpaceX’s record $86.2bn flotation, and Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are leading the listing.

]]> 2473793Lucy Mackenzie-Cheesewright Lucy Mackenzie-Cheesewright Mahmood waters down migration rules for care workers in £10bn gamble https://www.cityam.com/mahmood-waters-down-migration-rules-for-care-workers-in-10bn-gamble/ Mon, 02 Nov 2026 16:32:05 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2473775

Home secretary Shabana Mahmood has watered down migration rules for care workers after backlash from Labour MPs, although high earners will benefit from faster routes to settlement in the UK.  The home secretary confirmed plans to allow some entrepreneurs, scientists and workers earning above £125,141 a year to be granted settled status rights after three [...]]]>

Home secretary Shabana Mahmood has watered down migration rules for care workers after backlash from Labour MPs, although high earners will benefit from faster routes to settlement in the UK. 

The home secretary confirmed plans to allow some entrepreneurs, scientists and workers earning above £125,141 a year to be granted settled status rights after three years living in the UK in a contribution-based approach to immigration. 

Migrants who are granted indefinite leave to remain (ILR) are allowed to live in the UK for as long as they wish and gain broader access to Britain’s welfare system and change jobs without employers’ sponsorship. 

But after looking over 200,000 consultation entries for nearly a year, Mahmood announced that care workers who earned at least £25,000 a year will be able to gain ILR with their dependents after five years in the UK. People who arrived on fraudulent visas will have a “second chance” to apply for a real visa. 

She had previously said her restrictions on ILR time periods would apply retrospectively to hundreds of thousands of care workers who arrived after the pandemic.  Mahmood told parliament that 250,000 people and their dependents arrived or switched onto a previous special visa for the sector. 

Mahmood’s migration U-turn

The home secretary said that while she aimed to tackle abuse of the visa from some employers, she wished to recognise the “service of those who cared for our sick and elderly at a time of immense national need” during the pandemic. 

Mahmood’s decision to water down restrictions on ILR represents a significant change in tack since Andy Burnham rose to Number 10. Two Cabinet ministers, Miatta Fahnbulleh and Angela Rayner, had appeared to publicly criticise Mahmood’s proposals. The Home Secretary’s original proposal was seen as a tough approach to migration, but the plan sparked a furious row within the Labour party.

The U-turn is set to come under heavy scrutiny given concerns raised over the costs that some low-income migrant workers have on public services. The Conservatives pointed to government research stating that social workers and dependents settling in the UK between 2026 and 2030 alone would cost the taxpayer nearly £10bn over the course of workers’ lifetimes driven by welfare payments including the state pension.  

The cost of each social care worker on the taxpayer amounts to about £36,000 and £67,000 for each dependent, according to the Migration Advisory Committee.

Mahmood told MPs on Monday: “Everyone will have a fair shot to make their contribution, and no one will be punished for the sins of their employer. But we will also preserve the critical element of this reform: that settlement must be linked to contribution.”

Those earning above around £51,000 will be able to apply for ILR after five years in the UK while low-income workers will have to apply for settled status after 10 years. Previously, Mahmood had set out plans to make some low income workers wait for 15 years before getting ILR. 

Prior to Mahmood’s announcement, Burnham told ITV News that it was “difficult” to say whether net migration was too high or too low. 

“It’s got to be, if you like, following gaps in the economy. Because if you just put a number on it, then we may have a shortage in a certain area and then you’re saying, ‘Well, we can’t recruit people.”

The most recent set of official statistics showed that net migration was 171,000 in the year to December 2025. 

This has dropped from a peak of around 944,000 two years earlier, even as the last Conservative government pledged to slash migration.

The Commonwealth Games delivered more in economic activity than it cost to host as organisers proved the viability of a slimmed-down iteration of the event. The 2026 Commonwealth Games, which took place this summer in Glasgow, cost less than £160m to stage after the Scottish city stepped in for Victoria when the Australian state pulled [...]]]>

The Commonwealth Games delivered more in economic activity than it cost to host as organisers proved the viability of a slimmed-down iteration of the event.

The 2026 Commonwealth Games, which took place this summer in Glasgow, cost less than £160m to stage after the Scottish city stepped in for Victoria when the Australian state pulled out citing funding issues.

The 11-day competition generated £176m in economic value for Glasgow while the figure for the wider Scottish region was £223m. 

Commonwealth Games Scotland’s Ian Reid said: “Two years ago, when the future of these Games was uncertain, we believed Scotland could step forward and lead to provide a solution that could not only reset and secure the future of the Games but also deliver an outstanding event in a responsible and sustainable way, while showcasing our athletes on the world stage.

Commonwealth Games boost

“It was a reminder of what makes the Commonwealth Games so special. Everyone who worked tirelessly to deliver this altogether brilliant Games should be immensely proud.”

But any hopes of Scotland paving the way for smaller editions in the long term is likely to be dashed in four years’ time when India takes on hosting duties. Ahmedabad’s staging of the 2030 Commonwealth Games is seen as a rehearsal run for a future Olympic Games bid, backed by the mega-rich Ambani family.

Glasgow’s model, though, could set a precedent for nations unable to commit billions in funding to host the Games on a tight budget. It could see Nigeria push forward with a bid for the 2034 Games – where they are expected to be up against bids from East Africa and New Zealand. 

The race to host the 2034 Commonwealth Games is set to start in earnest next November, three years before India stages the next edition, which is set to feature the 132,000-capacity Narendra Modi Stadium at its centre.

]]> 2473776Matt Hardy Matt Hardy Global AI sell-off eases after bruising end of month performance https://www.cityam.com/global-ai-sell-off-eases-after-bruising-end-of-month-performance/ Mon, 02 Nov 2026 15:53:13 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2473696

The global AI sell-off eased on Monday as falling oil prices buoyed investors’ moods and sent them flocking back to tech stocks. The global AI sell-off eased on Monday as falling oil prices buoyed investors’ moods and sent them flocking back to tech stocks.

After a bruising rout in tech shares on Wall Street last week, the Nasdaq Composite Index and the S&P 500 rose 1.2 per cent and 0.7 respectively on market open.

It’s a sharp recovery for the Nasdaq Composite, which slipped 3.5 per cent on Friday, capping off its worst month in over a year. Roughly $3 trillion has been wiped off the tech-heavy index since its peak early last month.

Amazon rebounded from last week’s decline, which had been caused by weaker than expected sales, with a gain of 4.5 per cent.

Fellow Magnificent Seven companies Microsoft and Nvidia increased 0.6 per cent and 1.9 per cent respectively.

But chipmaker Intel, which led Friday’s losses after a gloomy forecast caused shares to plunge 28.5 per cent, failed to rebound on market open. Shares declined a further 2.2 per cent.

Ajay Rajadhyaksha, global chair of research at Barclays, said in a note to clients the “big call now is whether recent weeks are the first signs of an impending AI collapse”, though he added that “in general, earnings have remained healthy”.

Caution in Asia

Wall Street’s came after stocks recovered in Asia, with Saxo market strategist Neil Wilson saying the region’s tech stocks were “stabilising”.

South Korea’s blue-chip index increased 2.2 per cent, buoyed by heavyweights Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, which gained 3.1 per cent and 3.8 per cent respectively.

Hong Kong’s Hang Seng gained 0.4 per cent, while the Shanghai Composite rose 1.1 per cent.

But there were “soft spots”, including Japan’s Nikkei 225 which dropped 0.3 per cent. Losses were led by memory-chip manufacturer Kioxia which tumbled 15.7 per cent after its latest earnings update forecast that demand for its products is beginning to cool.

Fujitsu also extended last week’s losses, slipping 2.9 per cent to 3,514 yen (£16.5), and Open AI investor Soft Bank fell 1.5 per cent. This takes the group’s losses to 51 per cent from its June peak.

Energy reversal and midterms

The easing on stocks came amid falling energy prices. Brent crude, the international oil benchmark, fell 6.9 per cent to $106.4 per barrel. 

Patrick Munnelly, partner at Tickmill Group, said: “The primary macro relief valve came via energy markets. Brent crude slid… following reports that the White House favours extending diplomatic avenues with Tehran ahead of the US midterms before considering military escalation.”

Analysts are awaiting the outcome of the US midterms on Tuesday, with polls putting Republicans at risk of losing control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate. 

Some have warned that Trump could launch renewed attacks on Iran once the constraints of the election are over, ultimately sending oil prices higher once more.

Jason Hollands, managing director of Bestinvest, said that the performance of Democrats in the election could also cause AI stock’s rebound to end.

“AI is an area where the details will matter, especially as it has been such a major driver of financial markets in recent years, the power of which was evident in last week’s rout,” he said.

“Some Democrats have proposed making data-centre operators bear more of the electricity costs created by their projects. Any such change could affect the economics of new data centres and the wider AI investment boom.”

]]> 2473696Maisie Grice Maisie Grice Can Marks & Spencer’s TikTok star help it ‘dump the frump’? https://www.cityam.com/can-marks-spencers-tiktok-star-help-it-dump-the-frump/ Mon, 02 Nov 2026 15:42:16 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2473731

Marks & Spencer will face shareholders on Wednesday, with hopes of presenting a lift from its breakout social media star, Kathryn Turner, writes Felix Armstrong. Ditch the fake blood and vampire fangs: Britain’s viral Halloween costume this year featured a white shirt, a blue sweater vest and a blonde wig. Kathryn Turner, Marks & Spencer’s [...]]]>

Marks & Spencer will face shareholders on Wednesday, with hopes of presenting a lift from its breakout social media star, Kathryn Turner, writes Felix Armstrong.

Ditch the fake blood and vampire fangs: Britain’s viral Halloween costume this year featured a white shirt, a blue sweater vest and a blonde wig. Kathryn Turner, Marks & Spencer’s director of product development, has become a runaway social media star in recent months, and the retailer has quickly capitalised on her newfound Tiktok fame. 

Turner, dubbed this year’s top ‘gay Halloween’ costume, has soared in popularity in recent months after taking her followers inside M&S Food’s latest products, including candyfloss-flavoured grapes and chocolate and pistachio sandwiches. 

Since relaunching her social media profiles in May, Turner has garnered 281,000 followers on Instagram and a further 319,000 on TikTok, far more than the official M&S Food channel’s 270,000. She has worked at the retailer since 1995, and her breakthrough food creation was Tubby Toast, inspired by the children’s TV show Teletubbies, which first hit the shelves in 1998. 

But M&S’s latest social media star, whose fans include Nigella Lawson and Ian Wright, is not alone. The retailer has encouraged its staff to grow their individual profiles online, and the company says its employees run about 600 Facebook pages and 100 TikTok accounts offering viewers the inside scoop on its products. 

Richard Hyman, an independent retail analyst, said Kathryn Turner’s online profile has “clearly a very successful campaign” for the company. 

M&S Food is “performing very strongly and gaining market share,” he added. “It’s always a mistake to equate social media success with commercial progress, but this will have played its part.”

The grocer notched 10.7 per cent sales growth in the four weeks to October, according to the latest NIQ data. The analytics firm attributed this boost directly to Turner’s online presence. 

“M&S’ strong performance has been supported by growing social media interest in its product launches, with director of product development Kathryn Turner attracting attention on TikTok, reflecting the retailer’s ability to turn product buzz into shopper demand,” NIQ’s data experts said.

Clothing arm in need of a lift

Marks & Spencers has long been pushing to widen its Gen-Z audience after hiring Maddy Evans, formerly of Topshop, in 2023. The retailer hopes to provide more proof when it publishes its first-half results on Wednesday. 

At the company’s annual general meeting this summer, chief executive Stuart Machin told shareholders that the retailer has worked hard to develop its offering for younger customers, through collaborations with influencers like Amelia Dimoldenberg, declaring that it has successfully “dumped the frump”. 

The retailer celebrated its 100th anniversary in July by staging a catwalk show at London Fashion Week, in the latest sign that M&S is finally becoming cool. But Machin has reassured investors that he will not stray too far from the middle-class families which have long propped up the brand, saying his mother had reminded him its clothes were at risk of becoming “too skimpy”.

Hyman cautioned, however, that Turner’s efforts are mainly benefitting M&S’ food arm, while its clothing and home businesses are “finding life more challenging,” despite these efforts to dump the frump. 

This side of the company has been slower to recover from the cyber attack which ravaged the retailer in April last year, knocking £131m from its balance sheet. Sales in food, home and beauty fell by 7.7 per cent in the year to March, while food sales jumped by seven per cent.

The retailer told shareholders in May that its non-food arm was worse hit by the “temporary pause in online trading and systems access, which disrupted stock flow and restricted availability”. 

But analysts said M&S has made solid progress since last year’s cyberattack, and its share price has gained nearly 30 per cent in the last six months. As it tries to bring its clothing business up to speed with its food arm, the retailer may have benefited from a surge in sales of white shirts and blonde wigs this Halloween.

It is also a means of lifting the spirits of the 50,000-strong Ukrainian community in Greater London, many of whom were displaced by the war.

House builders and consumer groups are coming under pressure from short sellers as investors bet on a downturn across both sectors in the coming months.

The number of London-listed firms with over five per cent of their shares held short more than doubled from 27 to 60 in the three months to October, according to the latest analysis from law firm White & Case, while companies facing short positions of larger than 10 per cent rose to 14 from two.

Short positions are financial bets made by investors, often hedge funds, who predict that a company’s stock will decline. Investors borrow shares at their current price before selling with the aim of buying them back at a lower price in order to make a profit.

House builders, building materials manufacturers, and retail and consumer groups have borne the brunt of the pressure from investors. Builders accounted for five of the 14 companies with the highest disclosed short positions, led by Vistry, where investors currently hold short interest of 16.7 per cent.

This was closely followed by brick maker Ibstock, with investors holding a position of 12.9 per cent, after it was forced to lower its earnings target in response to “deteriorating” trading conditions.

Analysts have pinned the uptick in short positions on soaring material and construction costs and falling profit margins, which have forced many firms in the sector to forecast losses.

Sticky inflation and changes to consumer confidence caused by the rising cost of living also impacted London-listed retail companies. Investors held a position of 11.1 per cent in WH Smith, and 9.8 per cent in Ocado at the end of October.

Short-selling surge

Lawyers at White & Case urged firms to become aware of the increase in short-selling, encouraging them to “proactively engage with investors and analysts” before an alternative analysis of performance is released to the market.

“Shorting… has now reached new highs in UK public markets,” said Patrick Sarch, head of UK public M&A at White & Case.

“As short-selling becomes an increasingly prominent feature of the market, it should be treated by boards as a mainstream risk…with companies actively planning for, and not just reacting to, these pressures.”

Opportunities for short sellers have become increasingly attractive this year, as valuations have come under pressure from heightened geopolitical tension, market uncertainty and fears over AI-related disruption.

A number of housebuilders have slashed their profit targets and warned of a slowdown as they are buffeted by rising interest rates, a slowdown in the property market and rising red tape around building. In its assessment of the Budget last week, the Office for Budget Responsibility said housing delivery will fall to 229,000 this year, 221,000 the following year and to 219,000 in the year 2027-28.

The OBR had previously thought housing construction would pick up in this year, to 252,000, but said it has downgraded this outlook owing to rising costs of building and the burden of red tape on builders.

Retail groups are also set to feel the pressure of rising inflation. According to the Bank of England’s forecasts, inflation is set to top four per cent early next year. The Bank is set to hike interest rates this week for the first time in three years, in a move likely to squeeze spending consumers’ spending power further.

Sarch said he expected more companies to be exposed to short-selling in the run up to the end of 2026, but said “many will bounce back successfully”.

“At a macro level, shorting continues to play a healthy role in capital markets, supporting price discovery, liquidity, transparency and market discipline,” he said.

Regulatory overhaul

While broader macroeconomic problems were identified as the primary cause for the uptick in short-selling, some of the increase “may also reflect changes” made by the City watchdog, White & Case said.

Under the old regime, when any single fund built a short position of 0.5 per cent or more in a UK company, the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) would publish both the fund and the exact percentage. Lower positions were reported privately.

Funds typically faced scrutiny and ran the risk of being the aim of short squeezes, leaving many to cap their shorts at 0.49 per cent in a bid to avoid being on the list, while some opted not to short UK firms altogether.

In July 2026, the FCA overhauled the rules, no longer publishing the names of individual short sellers, instead only publishing the single, net short figure for each company. The removal of the spotlight enabled short sellers to take larger positions.

Meta, Tiktok and X will face a tougher battle resisting Ofcom’s demands for online safety data after the High Court ruled that tech giants must provide detailed evidence of compliance costs in order to challenge the regulator’s requests.

The judgment, handed down on Friday, strengthens Ofcom’s ability to demand information from social media platforms even before it has decided whether to pursue further regulatory action.

It follows an unsuccessful legal challenge by Meta, WhatsApp, X and Tiktok to notices requiring them to provide historical data on user activity, harmful content and moderation practices dating back to January 2024.

While the dismissal was revealed last week, the judgment sets out a significant hurdle for future challenges by refusing to allow companies to claim that information requests are excessive without demonstrating the additional work involved.

“A general assertion that less burdensome notices could have been issued without unduly detracting from their usefulness will not do”, the judges said.

Higher bar for legal challenges

The dispute centred on information notices issued by Ofcom in February under the Online Safety Act, requiring platforms to provide data on content moderation, user complaints, appeals and exposure to harmful material.

The companies argued that the demands exceeded Ofcom’s statutory powers, imposed disproportionate compliance costs and circumvented the Act’s separate transparency reporting regime.

But Justice Singh and Justice Collins Rice rejected those arguments, finding that Ofcom could gather information to inform future regulatory decisions without first identifying a specific investigation or proposed rule change.

The judges also found the companies had failed to demonstrate the additional resources required to comply with the notices, separate from costs they would incur under their existing obligations.

Their evidence “does not sufficiently identify the necessary baselines or differential resource impact”, the court said.

The ruling leaves the notices intact, although Ofcom must still ensure that future requests are proportionate to their intended purpose.

The decision marks the first judicial review testing the watchdog’s information-gathering powers under the Online Safety Act, which allows it to fine non-compliant companies up to £18m or 10 per cent of qualifying global annual turnover, whichever is higher.

Age checks adds to regulatory pressure

The ruling comes as tech firms face growing scrutiny over how they enforce Britain’s forthcoming ban on social media for under-16s.

Ofcom last week identified four methods of age verification it considers sufficiently reliable, including facial age estimation and banking-based checks.

The proposals have renewed debate over whether age verification should be handled by individual social media platforms or at the app-store and operating-system level.

Meta told City AM that it supported a layered approach involving app stores, arguing that repeated checks across different services could create unnecessary burdens for users.

The social media giant added that it already uses facial age estimation, ID checks and artificial intelligence to identify teenagers who may have misrepresented their ages.

Ofcom’s latest assessment found that all eight app stores it examined relied on users declaring their own ages, with additional verification used only in limited circumstances.

While the regulator has acknowledged that app stores could play a greater role, social media companies would remain responsible for meeting their own legal obligations.

The High Court’s decision does not determine how those age checks should be implemented, but it reinforces Ofcom’s ability to demand evidence from platforms as it assesses their compliance.

Meta said last week it was disappointed by the ruling, arguing that information-gathering on this scale went beyond what was necessary or proportionate. Tiktok said it was reviewing the judgment.

The tax authority is conducting an inquiry into how the consulting group determines whether its partners are technically self-employed or employees for income tax and national insurance contribution (NIC) purposes, according to BCG’s recent Companies House filings.

The consulting firm, which employs around 33,500 people globally, said in the filings it had hired external legal counsel to help examine its approach to the so-called salaried members rules, which apply to all firms that follow the LLP structure.

“The matter is under discussion, and the partnership has engaged external legal counsel who has affirmed the partnership’s position on the matter,” the filings said.

The consulting group added in the filings that if HMRC’s “position were ultimately upheld, the partnership could become liable for additional tax and any associated interest and penalties, which, depending on the outcome, could have a material impact on the financial statements.”

“The outcome, amount, and timing of this matter remain uncertain and cannot be reliably estimated,” the filings said.

The LLP model came into force over 25 years ago and is used by many firms across the professional services industry, including law firms, accountancy firms, and consultancies. It is a structure in which members, known as partners, invest their own capital, take on the risk, and in return, do not pay corporate tax on their profits.

A BCG spokesperson said in a statement: “We comply with all of our global and local tax obligations wherever we operate. As set out in our latest UK LLP accounts we are currently in discussion with HMRC and will not be commenting further while those discussions are ongoing.”

HMRC declined to comment.

Sarah Curzon, tax partner at MHA, told City AM the fresh inquiry “should make professional-services LLPs sit up and take notice.”

“The financial exposure from getting this wrong can be substantial once employer’s NIC, interest and potentially penalties are considered. Professional firms therefore need robust evidence supporting their position, not simply an LLP agreement that calls someone a partner,” Curzon said.

HMRC’s watchful eye after LLP tax ruling

The confirmation of HMRC’s probe into BCG comes after a landmark £200m Supreme Court ruling in July which sent shock waves through the City’s professional services industry.

Supreme Court judges ruled against hedge fund Blue Crest Capital Management, run by billionaire Michael Platt, and unanimously rejected the argument that its partners were technically self employed and therefore not subject to the same income tax and national insurance treatment as normal employees.

The court ruled that partners in a Limited Liability Partnership (LLPs) must be taxed as employees rather than as self-employed profit-sharers, leaving the hedge fund facing a near £200m tax bill as a result of the ruling.

Curzon said following the ruling, “this is clearly an area in which HMRC is prepared to challenge whether individuals described as partners genuinely meet the tax tests for partnership status.”

The flagship Alfa Romeo Giulia Quadrifolio is currently off-sale, but will be back soon – at a likely cost of around £85,000. It packs a 520hp Ferrari-derived V6 and is an altogether more serious proposition. You can read my review here.

The differences between the entry-level Sprint and my long-term Veloce essentially come down to equipment. Standard kit on the Sprint includes 18-inch alloy wheels, automatic high-beam headlights, front/rear parking sensors and an 8.8-inch touchscreen with wired smartphone connectivity via Apple CarPlay or Android Auto.

Spending the extra £5,000 on the Giulia Veloce gets you 19-inch rims, leather upholstery, a limited-slip differential, red brake calipers, tinted rear windows, heated electric seats and a heated steering wheel. 

Still a great-looking saloon

My Veloce only has a couple of options fitted: an electric panoramic sunroof (£1,250) and Montreal Green metallic paint (£2,000), bringing its total cost to £50,575. 

Montreal Green is easily the most expensive paint choice (only Alfa Red is free, the others are £500-£850), but I reckon it’s worth the hefty outlay. In the soft autumn sunshine it looks deep and lustrous, really setting off the Veloce’s shapely ‘Dark Petal’ wheels. 

Indeed, even at more than a decade old – pensionable in automotive terms – the Giulia is still a looker. Its classic proportions and elegant curves contrast with the more angular, aggressive aesthetic of German rivals. Alfa Romeo’s trad shield grille and offset number plate are instantly identifiable, too. A couple of strangers have already commented “nice car”, which wouldn’t happen with a BMW 3 Series.

Reason enough to buy one? No, but it certainly provides a warm feeling when you see it on the driveway. The artist and writer William Morris said: “Have nothing in your house that you do not know to be useful, or believe to be beautiful”. The Alfa Romeo seems to tick both boxes.

Inside the Giulia Veloce

The Giulia’s interior is also attractively designed, with nods to classic Alfas such as the hooded instrument binnacle (still with analogue dials, rather than the now-usual digital screen) and ribbed leather trim. The three-spoke steering wheel and long, supercar-style metal shift paddles are very tactile, too.

You sit low, which immediately makes the car feel snug and driver-focused, while the six-way adjustable seats are very supportive. After the rather lofty driving position of the Renault 5 – necessitated by the battery pack beneath its floor – this is a refreshing reset.

Negative points? The Alfa’s rear legroom isn’t as generous as some mid-sized saloons and some of the plastics aren’t exactly ‘premium’. The infotainment system also looks a bit dated, and makes deactivating the driver assistance (ADAS) bleeps more complicated than necessary. You can operate it via the 8.8-inch touchscreen or a clickwheel on the centre console.

Time to hit the road

In terms of numbers, the Veloce will sprint to 62mph in 5.7 seconds and reach a top speed of 149mph. Drive with a bit less brio and you might see 37.7mpg, while official CO2 emissions are 169g/km. That equates to road tax of £1,410 in the first year, then £640 for five years thereafter (including the ‘expensive car supplement’ that applies to anything with a list price above £40,000).

I will be keeping track of the Alfa’s efficiency and reporting back on how it drives. Arriving in October might seem sub-optimal for a rear-driven sports saloon, but I’m looking forward to a real-world test. Bring on the British winter. Frosty mornings, wet roundabouts and slippery second-gear corners: I’m ready for you.

    If Labour doesn’t respect the rules of Parliament, including secrecy, why should anyone else, asks Eliot Wilson

    The Victorian journalist Walter Bagehot, who wrote The English Constitution in 1865-67, drew a critical distinction between the parts of our constitutional arrangements which were “dignified” and those that were “efficient”. The monarchy and the House of Lords fell into the first category, while the second included the executive and the House of Commons. The dignified parts might be rich in ceremonial grandeur; but the efficient parts actually operated the machinery of state.

    Last week’s Budget Day demonstrated that it is rapidly moving from efficient to dignified. We dwell heavily on the lore: the photo opportunity for the Chancellor and Treasury ministers outside 11 Downing Street, at which he holds up the ministerial red box containing his speech; the fact he can enjoy an alcoholic drink at the despatch box (though none has for 30 years); the quasi-religious secrecy surrounding the whole process.

    That last part, the secrecy, is now a joke. It represents a serious challenge to the way we do politics.

    This year, like last year and the year before, the measures contained in the Budget were meticulously and comprehensively briefed to the media in the days running up to Budget Day. Five days in advance, Politico was confidently analysing what Labour Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey would announce, and some of the information was explicitly attributed to “current… government officials”.

    In 2025, the government dropped any pretence of propriety. The Chancellor, Rachel Reeves, gave a “scene setter” speech three weeks in advance of the Budget, while HM Treasury published a press release three days beforehand which – bizarrely – announced changes to the state pension which were “expected” to be made, but included verbatim quotes from Reeves.

    The rules governing this are not ambiguous. The Ministerial Code, which sets out the standards expected of ministers and which was updated only a year ago, states the general principle: “When Parliament is in session, the most important announcements of government policy should be made in the first instance in Parliament.”

    In addition, a Resolution of the House of Commons of 19 March 1997 required that “Ministers should be as open as possible with Parliament”.

    We still talk gravely about the importance of secrecy. In November 1947, on his way into the House of Commons at around 3.15pm to deliver the Budget, the Chancellor, Hugh Dalton, stopped; rarely able to resist an indiscretion, he took John Carvel of The London Star to one side and gave him a few details of what he was about to say. Dalton rose to begin his Financial Statement at 3.32 pm, within about 20 minutes of the conversation. But details were in late editions of the Star on sale by 3.45 pm, while the Chancellor was still on his feet.

    The premature disclosure had no financial effects, but Dalton apologised to the House the following afternoon for his “grave indiscretion”. Following a meeting with the Prime Minister, Clement Attlee, that evening, both accepted that the Chancellor had to resign. A principle had been breached: the contents of the Budget had to be presented to the House of Commons before anyone else. There could be no exceptions. 

    Today Dalton would be a woeful underachiever.

    This is not just an issue of going against some arbitrary words in the Ministerial Code. There are many reasons why ministers should make announcements to Parliament before anywhere else. As a matter of principle, the House of Commons is, as Enoch Powell described it, “the personification of the people of Britain” and, as it has sole control over taxation and expenditure, it must be informed of changes to those areas before anyone else.

    The consequences of leaking

    There is also a practical political point. If the government, for media management reasons, reveals major parts of the Budget in statements or speeches outside Parliament, it avoids proper scrutiny: no demands for more detail, no exposure of flawed assumptions or unintended consequences. Ministers are evading or deferring questions from elected Members of Parliament.

    More broadly, leaking, whether deliberately by the government or on a freelance basis by ministers and others, is corrosive to Whitehall’s decision-making process. It eats away at trust. Ministers and officials will hold back and self-censor if they fear every word could be on social media within an hour. Under the last government, Cabinet became a cipher, irrelevant to policy and execution, because some ministers were so leaky that discussions appeared in the media virtually in real time. It pushed serious debate and decision-making elsewhere.

    In the end, high-handed media briefing by the government damages Parliament, not an institution with much reputational resilience at present. Sir Keir Starmer clearly found the House of Commons a frustrating impertinence, setting the tone for his Labour administration. Andy Burnham’s accession has yet to move the needle.

    Of course previous Conservative governments have behaved shoddily towards Parliament too. But now it seems deliberate policy to fall short of the bare minimum required. Ministers consistently make major announcements without informing the House first and sit mutely while the Speaker – rightly – admonishes them. More than half of all MPs were elected in 2024 or since, and many of them are eager to be anywhere except the Commons and to do anything but their jobs as legislators.

    If Parliament has a poor reputation, if it is seen as weak and malleable, there is one guaranteed winner – the government. In theory, Parliament is supreme: the Budget embodies the fact that the government cannot spend a sou, cannot access its bank account without the consent of Parliament. But all of that is a nullity if Parliament looks the other way.

    Parliament is not perfect, but it is the best check on the government and the best voice of the nation we have. It has been doing that for 750 years, and the most entrenched sceptic would feel its sudden absence. It should be taken seriously, but if the government tries to ignore it at every turn and MPs don’t want to be there, what is a jaded and exhausted electorate supposed to think?

    Eliot Wilson is a writer and historian. He is a senior fellow for national security at the Coalition for Global Prosperity and a contributing editor at Defence on the Brink

    Tesco’s sale of its Czech and Slovak businesses is the latest step in its long retreat from a once-sprawling global presence. Felix Armstrong traces this journey

    Tesco’s hold on the British grocery market is unmatched. Holding a towering 27.8 per cent market share across more than 3,600 shops, the supermarket chain is a fixture on high streets and retail parks across the UK. 

    But the UK was once just a small part of the grocer’s global geographic footprint, spanning Arizona to Malaysia.

    The firm’s ambitions for expansion across the world had once been sky-high. In 2007, then-chief executive Sir Terry Leahy said there was nowhere the grocer wouldn’t go. “We are on the threshold of becoming one of the few successful international retailers. There’s plenty to do,” he had said. 

    Under the stewardship of Ken Murphy, however, Tesco performed a handbrake turn. The group has gradually retreated from more than a dozen international markets, as its boss focuses his efforts on pushing down prices and improving quality at home.

    The far-flung countries from which Tesco has packed up its belongings in recent years include Poland, Thailand, China, Turkey, Pakistan, the US, Hong Kong and South Korea.

    And following the FTSE 100 group’s £1.5bn sale of its businesses in the Czech Republic and Slovakia, just one trace remains of Tesco’s globetrotting escapade: Hungary.   

    Murphy told shareholders on Friday that it had been “a privilege to serve customers” in the Czech Republic and Slovakia, adding that he was “proud” of what Tesco had achieved in the two markets. 

    But he said the sale of these two businesses will allow the grocery chain to double down on its “core UK and Irish businesses and [support] our continued investment in our food-first retail ecosystem and the capabilities that will drive future growth, while enabling a further return of capital to shareholders”. 

    Tesco first acquired its store estate in these two countries as a by-product of its exit from Taiwan, when it swapped its footprint in the East Asian state with French retailer Carrefour’s shops in the Czech Republic and Slovakia.

    Last year, Tesco’s operations in these two countries accounted for £2.9bn in revenue, across their combined 363 locations.

    Orbán to blame?

    The grocer had been expecting to offload its Hungarian arm as part of a wholesale exit from central Europe, but it said on Friday that it is continuing to “review all options for the future of [its] business in Hungary”.

    It is unclear whether Tesco offered its Hungarian operations to Ahold Delhaize, the Dutch supermarket which picked up the rest of its European arm, or whether the grocer has opted to retain its last outpost on the continent.

    Charles Allen, an analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, said he thinks Tesco “would like” to sell its business in Hungary but is being blocked from doing so by the heavy tax burden which faces retailers in this market. 

    Hungarian Prime Minister Victor Orbán has led a campaign against foreign-owned food sellers in recent years. In 2022, his government slapped a 4.5 per cent tax on revenues generated by these firms, along with a requirement to lower the prices of a number of staple foods.

    In March last year, Orban capped grocery markups on 30 basic food items – including eggs, milk and meat – at 10 per cent above wholesale costs in a bid to clamp down on rampant inflation.

    Supermarket chains including Austrian-owned Spar have hit out at the Hungarian government for its “devastating” tax hikes, appealing to the European Union to intervene.

    The 4.5 per cent tax has “pushed many chains into loss,” Allen said. He suggested that Tesco has adopted a ‘wait-and-see’ approach in the hopes that measures to soften these pressures could make the Hungarian market “more investor friendly.”

    Tesco told shareholders on Friday that its businesses in the Czech Republic and Slovakia account for the “majority” of the £119m underlying profit generated by its central European arm, suggesting that its stores in Hungary are feeling the pinch.

    Selling off its Hungarian outpost would leave Tesco with only Ireland as its sole territory outside the UK, where it controls roughly a quarter of the market. But given Murphy’s Cork roots, that arm of the business is going nowhere fast.
