]]> Gallium Defence, a Paris-based startup working on drone detection at a fraction of the cost of legacy systems, has emerged from stealth with a €7.1 million Seed funding round.

The round was led by Keen Venture Partners and 360 Capital, with participation from Omnes Capital and Polytechnique Ventures. This announcement coincided with European Defence Week 2026, held from 2nd to 6th November in Paris. 

“Great defence starts with superior visibility. Gallium Defence has the team, the industrial partners and the cost model to make drone detection a standard layer at every critical site – the kind of European capability our fund is proud to back,” said Alexander Ribbink, General Partner, Keen Venture Partners.

Gallium Defence was founded in April 2026 by Eric Fournier, Florian Lemoine, and Robin Mandel, three individuals with defence and industrial backgrounds. Fournier spent 17 years advising defence and aerospace leaders at Boston Consulting Group, while Lemoine has over 15 years’ experience in defence and served as a former adviser to NATO SACT. Mandel also brings over 15 years’ experience across industry and consulting through roles at Thales, BCG and Safran.

The company says more than 80% of critical infrastructure sites and military assets remain exposed to modern drone threats because of lack of affordable, field-ready radars capable of addressing the threat at scale. Gallium Defence was formed to address this gap by making high-performance radars affordable and easier to deploy, for both air security and air defence.

“As drones proliferate, traditional radars are reaching their operational and economic limits. At Gallium Defence, we started from a blank sheet with a simple question, asked by operators in the field: how do you meet 80% of the need at 20% of the price? Our answer: a radically rethought AESA radar architecture that makes extensive use of commercial off-the-shelf components and the power of embedded computing,” said Fournier, CEO and co-founder of Gallium Defence.

Gallium’s flagship product is called the GDS-10, an X-band AESA radar with a software-defined, AI-native architecture. It is designed for dual use and comes in two versions: one for critical infrastructure operators and one for armed forces.

The GDS-10 is capable of detecting Class 1 and FPV drones at a range of 10km. It provides 360° azimuth coverage and 90° elevation coverage with no blind spots, and can track multiple drones simultaneously, including within a swarm, day and night, in all weather conditions. Since GDS-10 is software-defined by design, its capabilities can evolve as new threats emerge.

“Our radars are designed to be manufactured and deployed by the hundreds, not one at a time,” said Mandel, COO and co-founder of Gallium Defence.

Just four months after closing its Seed round, the company conducted its first open-air field trials. The funding is being used to industrialise production of its first products, strengthen the team, train AI models, and run demonstrations for civil and military operators around the world. 

With the Seed funding raised and monthly field demonstrations underway, Gallium Defence is pitching itself as the sovereign European answer for drone detection at scale. The company plans to open orders for the GDS-10 in the first quarter of 2027.

]]> Marble Cognition (Marble), a Munich-based startup building AI coworkers that understand how work is executed to optimise and automate business operations, has raised €3.35 million ($3.75 million) in a pre-Seed round. 

The round was co-led by Heartcore and Seedcamp, with participation from angels including a board member of Datadog, a founder of Personio, and executives from McKinsey, Mistral AI and Lovable. The funding will scale inference, grow the engineering team in Munich, and support a US launch.

Reshma Sohoni, General Partner at Seedcamp, said, “Seedcamp has a long tradition of backing founders who change how we work, from UiPath and Synthesia to Marble today. Most companies want to automate more, but the hard part has always been mapping out how the work gets done. Marble fills that gap, giving companies vital context for AI transformations that could define their future. We’re proud to back them from the start.”

Marble Cognition was founded in late 2025 by Felix Rösner and Christophe Schmit, who met at Munich’s CDTM programme. The company states that it learns how work actually gets done inside a company, turns it into systems AI can read, and then deploys Marble Coworkers: AI agents that take over manual white-collar work. 

The company highlighted that, in an era when software is becoming a commodity, and so is building AI agents, the real value lies in knowing exactly what to automate. However, it notes that this is difficult, because every company runs on processes nobody has written down.

“McKinsey estimates that today’s technology could, in theory, automate about 57% of US work hours. Yet in almost every company Marble works with, around 90% of core processes live only in inboxes, spreadsheets and the heads of the people doing them. That, not the technology, is the biggest blocker to AI transformation. What is missing is an exact picture of how the work is done,” the German startup mentioned in the press release. 

Marble claims to build that picture. It observes how teams work, turning every process into a structured map that AI can read like code. It then builds Marble Coworkers that run the process end to end in the tools teams already use, with humans in the loop where judgement matters. 

It argues that traditional automation bends a standard product to fit a company’s processes. Marble states that it productises the understanding of the process itself.

Explaining its privacy and security measures, Marble says it anonymises everything it captures before any person or AI model sees it, even in the customer’s own cloud. Marble’s desktop app records screen activity, clicks, and keystrokes in the business apps people use at work, never private apps, private tabs, or anything outside working hours. It further notes that employees can pause it at any time, and data is only analysed in aggregate, not based on individuals.

“Every company we talk to wants AI to take over real work. But nobody can tell the AI how that work is actually done. So we solve that first. Our Coworkers watch how the work happens before they take it over. They do it the way your best people do,” said Rösner.

The technology relies on a containerised, plug-and-play system that uses a forward osmosis process to achieve Zero Liquid Discharge, meaning nothing is returned to the ocean. This system is designed to integrate into existing plant infrastructure without requiring operational downtime or upfront capital expenditure from plant operators.

Seamoretech says its system doubles freshwater production yield, cuts energy consumption by 50% compared with reverse osmosis, reduces operating costs by 30%, and lowers carbon emissions by up to 80% relative to conventional mineral mining.

Unlike other CleanTech startups, Seamoretech is not only working to accelerate the climate transition but also addressing two of Europe’s major priorities: water scarcity and securing domestic supply of critical raw materials. By recovering minerals such as lithium and magnesium from a local, fully traceable source, Seamoretech is showing the critical impact of its technology.

The new funding will be used for Seamoretech’s next phase of industrialisation and support its commercial expansion, including a planned launch in Spain next year. The company has already demonstrated collaboration in Spain and is now building a pipeline of pilot projects across several markets, including Spain and Egypt.

The startup plans to open a second closing of its Seed round in the coming months. ]]> The Netherlands has long been regarded as a European leader in agricultural and food innovation, but that position appears to be under threat.

A new report published today by Dutch national investment institution Invest-NL warns that the country risks losing its competitive edge as other nations move faster to commercialise emerging agricultural technologies.

According to the report, Deep Dive Agrifood Biotech, addressing the barriers facing Dutch agrifood biotechnology companies could unlock approximately €17 billion in additional annual revenue by 2040. However, without coordinated action on regulation, financing and commercialisation, much of that opportunity could be captured elsewhere.

Based on interviews with more than 150 entrepreneurs, investors, researchers and policymakers, alongside investment data spanning 2010 to April 2026, the study examines three strategic areas: seed breeding and genetics, biological agricultural inputs, and biotech-derived food ingredients.

A strong start, a weaker finish

The Netherlands is home to notable agricultural research institutions, established seed breeders and a sophisticated food production ecosystem. Yet it seems scientific excellence is not necessarily translating into globally competitive businesses.

The report highlights a particularly telling imbalance: the Netherlands accounts for 3.3% of BioTech startups worldwide, but only 1.3% of scale-ups, according to broader BioTech data cited from the Netherlands Organisation for Applied Scientific Research (TNO). This suggests that while the country remains effective at generating innovation, it is less successful at helping young companies achieve meaningful commercial scale.

Invest-NL identifies three recurring weaknesses:

  • too few promising technologies become scalable ventures
  • regulatory and validation processes delay market entry
  • insufficient financing prevents companies from reaching industrial production

The stakes extend beyond individual businesses. In a favourable scenario, Invest-NL estimates that annual Dutch agrifood BioTech revenues could reach approximately €25 billion by 2040, compared with just €8–9 billion if current conditions persist.

Crucially, the report argues that the Netherlands does not need to manufacture everything domestically. Instead, it should focus on retaining strategically valuable knowledge, intellectual property, companies and specialised capabilities, while taking advantage of European production networks where appropriate.

Ten years to say yes

One of the most striking obstacles concerns biological crop protection, where Dutch companies are developing alternatives to conventional chemical pesticides.

Obtaining European regulatory approval for a new biological crop protection product can take eight to ten years. Existing frameworks were largely designed around chemical products, making them less suited to certain biological innovations.

Consequently, some companies prioritise launching in markets such as Brazil and the United States, where commercialisation can proceed more quickly. Invest-NL warns that Europe risks losing ground in a biological crop protection market that could expand seven- to tenfold by 2040.

Food biotechnology faces similar difficulties. Regulatory approval for novel ingredients can take one to three years longer in Europe than in the United States, while building a first commercial production facility can require tens or even hundreds of millions of euros.

For fermentation-derived food ingredients alone, Invest-NL estimates that favourable conditions could support approximately €8 billion in annual Dutch revenues by 2040, compared with around €2 billion under existing policies.

The report stresses that faster approvals should not come at the expense of safety. Instead, regulators should offer earlier guidance, more predictable assessments and opportunities for companies to validate products under real-world conditions.

Innovation is not the issue

Recent EU-Startups coverage demonstrates that Dutch AgriTech entrepreneurs continue to attract investor interest across several areas identified in the report.

In August, Eindhoven-based VitalFluid secured €17.2 million to accelerate the commercialisation of its plasma-activated water technology, which offers growers an alternative to chemical crop protection. The investment was co-led by Invest-NL and Alder Tree Investments.

Meanwhile, Wageningen-based Aardaia raised €5 million in July to advance its genomics-driven crop breeding platform and develop a protein-rich tuber, while Nijmegen-based Gravity Gardens secured €2.6 million in September to scale its chemical-free seed activation technology.

Dutch food BioTech is also producing notable funding announcements. In June, Vivici received €12.5 million in European Innovation Council backing to expand the supply and commercial reach of its precision-fermented dairy proteins.

Last year, EU-Startups also reported on Revyve’s nearly €24 million Series B to expand production of yeast-based ingredients that can replace eggs in food manufacturing. Revyve had already commissioned a first-of-a-kind production facility in the Netherlands, illustrating that industrial scale-up is achievable with sustained backing.

Nevertheless, these successes do not eliminate the wider structural challenges. They illustrate the breadth of Dutch innovation, but also the importance of providing companies with appropriate financing and support beyond their initial funding rounds.

Europe will not wait

Across Europe, EU-Startups has reported comparable investment activity, illustrating how competition is developing around the same technologies.

In biological crop protection, France’s Agriodor raised €15 million in April to expand its natural scent-based pest management technology, while Denmark’s Mycoverse secured €2.4 million in March to develop fungal alternatives to chemical pesticides.

The competition is equally visible in food ingredients. French precision fermentation startups Verley raised €32 million and Standing Ovation secured €30 million in 2026, while Belgian fermentation company MAASH obtained a €12.15 million financing package combining equity and public financing to support industrial-scale mycoprotein production.

These announcements do not establish that the Netherlands has already lost its position. They do, however, show that European competitors are securing capital, developing production capacity and pursuing commercial opportunities in precisely the areas where Invest-NL sees significant Dutch potential.

To respond, Invest-NL proposes an indicative €650 million to €1.1 billion in public financing capacity between 2026 and 2030, spanning research, regulatory improvements, infrastructure and industrial scale-up.

Its ambitions for 2030 include doubling the number of agrifood BioTech ventures, reducing time to market by a factor of three, and developing five globally competitive companies capable of raising more than €100 million each.

For the Netherlands, the question is therefore becoming less about whether it can develop the next generation of agricultural technologies, and more about whether it can create the conditions for those technologies to become successful businesses.

]]> Talky Labs, a Spanish startup developing AI-powered technology to automate accounting and financial operations, has raised €1.5 million in a pre-Seed funding round to support team expansion, further product development and improvements to the company’s technical infrastructure.

The investment, closed in September 2026, saw participation from venture capital firms HelloWorld, Silence VC, Motive Force, and Aera Capital. Alongside angel investors Sebastián Gunningham; CEO of Remitly, Paul Golbaum; CEO of Lightbase and former CTO of Seedtag, and Javier Morenés, among others.

“Two years ago, I met my co-founder Jorge Beamonte at a networking event. That night, I called my mom and told her: ‘Mom, today is the most important day of my life. Everything is about to change,‘” said Maximilian Letón in a public statement.

Talky’s funding comes amid a series of European investments in AI-powered accounting and financial operations during 2026.

In Belgium, Dytto raised €1.5 million to develop its AI assistant for accountants, while Denmark’s Plinto secured €2.9 million for automated financial controls. Germany’s mika raised €6 million for AI-powered accounting and tax services, and UK-based Zalos obtained €3.1 million for enterprise finance automation.

In Spain, Barcelona-based Dolfin secured €2.1 million for adjacent financial workflows.

Together these rounds amount to approximately €66.8 million, including Talky’s investment.

“Every company has its own way of doing accounting, and it’s almost never written down. Talky learns those criteria, applies them to the hard cases and turns them into information for better decisions,” adds Jorge Beamonte, co-founder and CEO of Talky.

Founded in 2025 by Jorge Beamonte; CEO, and Maximilian Letón (23); COO, Talky aims to help businesses automate financial processes that traditionally depend on accountants’ experience and knowledge of internal company practices. Despite operating with a team of just nine employees, the startup reports having processed more than 1.8 million documents and over €2 billion in client expenditure through its platform.

The company addresses a common challenge in corporate finance departments: accounting decisions often rely on information scattered across enterprise systems, spreadsheets, emails, contracts and individual employees’ knowledge. While conventional automation tools can process standard transactions, unusual invoices or exceptions frequently require manual intervention, creating delays and increasing the risk of errors.

Talky’s platform uses AI to learn from a company’s historical accounting records and the expertise of its financial teams. Rather than relying exclusively on predefined rules, its technology identifies how previous transactions were handled, extracts relevant accounting criteria and applies that knowledge to new financial operations.

When the system encounters an unfamiliar situation or lacks sufficient information to make a decision, it identifies the appropriate employee to consult.

According to the startup, its technology processes between 86% and 93% of accounting documents without human intervention. The platform can read invoices, suggest accounting entries, review tax information and reconcile bank transactions before recording the results in the client’s enterprise resource planning (ERP) system.

The funding comes as Talky looks to expand its presence among large enterprises and financial services providers managing high volumes of transactions. Its founders have identified recruitment as a central priority, with plans to grow the team while continuing to develop the platform alongside existing customers.

AGN https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/ Aerospace Global News Mon, 02 Nov 2026 20:03:46 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.4 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/cropped-AGN_Icon_Jet-32x32.png AGN https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/ 32 32 Learjet 60 crash: Was a black box on board, and could it survive the impact? https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/florida-learjet-60-crash-black-box-recovery/ Mon, 02 Nov 2026 20:03:45 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=55316 Investigators face a difficult recovery effort after the Florida Learjet crash, with uncertainty over whether a cockpit voice recorder remained aboard.

The post Learjet 60 crash: Was a black box on board, and could it survive the impact? appeared first on AGN.

]]>

In any accident investigation, locating the so-called ‘black box’ can provide crucial details to help piece together the sequence of events.

The aircraft black box is actually two devices: the cockpit voice recorder (CVR) and the flight data recorder (FDR). Larger airlines need to have both installed.

But in the case of the fatal Learjet 60 crash in Florida, the rules around these black boxes are more opaque.

In the first press conference since the tragedy, National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) member Tom Chapman explained that the aircraft’s maintenance records suggested a CVR, at least, was installed.

“Our indication early here from aircraft maintenance records is that a cockpit voice recorder was installed on this aircraft,” he said.

“What we don’t know is whether that recorder was still on board; sometimes these things change over time.”

The NTSB said that the Learjet had potentially begun breaking up before impacting the ground, but refrained from speculating as to any possible cause. Chapman admitted that due to the high speeds involved, recovering meaningful parts would be a “real challenge.”

With a substantial part of the wreckage buried in a crater that is now filled with water, locating a data recorder could be vital to discovering what went wrong.

Did the Learjet carry the important ‘black box’ recorders?

During the press conference, Chapman confirmed that the Learjet was operated by Aurora Aviation, doing business as Upper Jets. It is a Part 135 operator, offering private jet flights on-demand.

Unlike commercial airlines, which operate under the FAA’s Part 121 rules, Part 135 operators are not always required to have both black boxes installed. For example, the FDR, which records flight parameters such as altitude and speed, is generally only required in aircraft with ten or more seats.

A previous sales listing for N722BD, the Learjet 60 involved in the crash, shows an eight-passenger layout inside. That puts it below the threshold required for a mandatory FDR, although some operators install them voluntarily.

However, Part 135 operators do require a cockpit voice recorder, or CVR, on multiengine turbine aircraft configured with six or more passenger seats when two pilots are required. The Learjet 60 does require two pilots.

As the NTSB stated, the aircraft’s maintenance records indicated it did have a CVR installed, and the sales listing also mentions a Universal CVR-30 cockpit voice recorder among its equipment. But it’s possible that it was subsequently removed before the accident.

“We’re still seeking to determine whether there was a recorder, and then of course we’re very hopeful that we can recover it,” Chapman explained. “It’s too early to know, but that’ll be very important data.”

Could a cockpit voice recorder survive the impact?

The Learjet crash was one of the most violent aviation incidents in recent memory. The speeds involved bent asphalt on impact and created a huge crater in the ground. The aircraft fragmented into thousands of tiny parts, which a team is now attempting to round up and recover.

Not all the debris is near the crater, however, with much spread around the neighbourhood, making progress laborious. Speaking at the media briefing, senior investigator Timothy Monville said of the crash site,

“I’m getting conflicting information. It’s probably a half mile by four tenths of a mile. But it’s scattered among ball fields, businesses, personal residences, and the debris is rather small.”

If the aircraft did carry a CVR, even a devastating crash such as this does not mean all data has been lost forever. Cockpit voice recorders are designed to protect their recordings against severe impact and fire. Even extensive damage to the recorder’s outer casing does not necessarily mean its contents are destroyed.

Nevertheless, questions remain over whether it was even on board at the time of the crash, and locating it is going to be a tough job.

“We’ll be better off with it,” Chapman admitted. “But even without it, our folks are very, very good. We’re still able to do some incredible detective work and determine how things transpired.”

]]> Florida Learjet crash: NTSB probes evidence aircraft broke up before impact https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/ntsb-investigating-possible-in-flight-breakup-florida-learjet-crash/ Mon, 02 Nov 2026 19:21:41 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=55299 Investigators say there is evidence the Learjet 60 may have broken up before impact, as they examine weather conditions and search for clues to the fatal crash.

The post Florida Learjet crash: NTSB probes evidence aircraft broke up before impact appeared first on AGN.

]]>
In Brief 4 min read
  • NTSB found evidence suggesting the Learjet may have begun breaking up before impact.
  • Weather, including reported icing and turbulence, is a major investigation focus.
  • Investigators are searching a widespread debris field, and have asked for help from the public.

Federal investigators are examining evidence that a Learjet 60 may have begun breaking apart before crashing in Florida and killing all nine people on board.

Speaking at a briefing on 2 November, Tom Chapman, a board member with the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB), said investigators have found “some evidence that there was some breakup of the aircraft before impact” and have identified debris beyond the main crash site.

Timothy Monville, senior investigator at NTSB, said: “The biggest obstacle that we’re going to have is recovering the major wreckage from the impacted crater on the roadway.”

Footage circulating on social media have prompted speculation about whether parts of the aircraft separated during its final descent. However, investigators have not confirmed which components, if any, detached before impact.

Chapman added: “We do have some indication that the aircraft was breaking up before impact, and so some of this is yet to be determined.

“We may find parts of the aircraft some distance away from the actual impact site. We’re finding debris, but we haven’t identified parts yet. That is going to be a real challenge.”

And he called on members of the public to let them know if they find any of the plane parts, saying: “I want to note that if members of the community find debris, please do not move it. Contact us or local authorities, and we will respond appropriately.”

Weather also a focus of the NTSB investigation

The aircraft, operated by Upper Jets under Part 135 charter regulations, departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport carrying two crew members and seven passengers bound for North Eleuthera in the Bahamas.

About two hours later, the crew reported light icing and moderate turbulence at 35,000ft before requesting a climb to 37,000ft due to increasing precipitation.

Less than 30 seconds after receiving clearance to climb, the crew reported a rapid descent and declared a mayday, later transmitting that the aircraft was in an overspeed condition before communications were lost.

Chapman said weather conditions are “a major focus of the investigation”, with specialists working to determine what conditions the aircraft encountered at altitude.

How thunderstorms affect aircraft at cruising altitude How thunderstorms affect aircraft at cruising altitude

Chapman added, “I’m told that the weather has been pretty crazy here lately, so that’s something we’re going to be concerned about.”

Co-pilot identified as investigation continues

The co-pilot of the Learjet 60 has been named as 20-year-old Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras. Her family confirmed to multiple US media outlets that she was among those killed in the crash.

Nathalia got her first pilot license in 2023 when she was 17. Speaking to local radio CBS12 at the time, she said: “I definitely do brag because people say, ‘Oh, you can’t drive,’ and I’m like, ‘Yeah, but I can fly.’”

Her mother Camila told The New York Times, “She loved the freedom. It was completely different seeing the world from the top.”

The identities of the pilot and passengers haven’t been released.

Calls for patience as speculation grows

Former astronaut Jared Isaacman urged observers to avoid drawing conclusions before investigators complete their work.

Posting on X, he wrote: “You do not know the aircraft’s maintenance history, whether there was a structural failure, if any failure was induced by turbulence, overspeed, or overcontrol, or everything happening in that cockpit,” he wrote.

“Let people investigate, learn, and share the facts. Be respectful to those who perished and the families who carry their memories.”

Writing this in my personal capacity, but I have been flying these types of aircraft for more than 20 years, with over 8,000 hours, and have reasonable familiarity with how the charter world operates. I feel compelled to post after seeing commentary about the Lear 60 crash, from missile strikes to DEI to critiquing this poor woman’s final radio calls. That last part is what I find most troubling. She was the second-in-command (SIC), and while she was empowered to point out mistakes as part of good crew resource management, she was doing her job, communicating with ATC right to the end in a terrifying situation. She likely knew before many of those calls that she was going to die. I have heard final calls from friends, from military pilots with thousands of hours in fighter aircraft, and they are just as heartbreaking because they know the end is approaching. I understand the public interest given the footage and audio. But you do not know the aircraft’s maintenance history, whether there was a structural failure, if any failure was induced by turbulence, overspeed, or overcontrol, or everything happening in that cockpit. I am sure weather will be part of the investigation, but beyond that, it is speculation. The charter industry routinely hires commercial pilots very early in their careers to gain experience alongside an ATP-qualified captain before they move up to the airlines. She would still have the appropriate training, qualifications, and checkouts by an FAA examiner or designee. Let people investigate, learn, and share the facts. Be respectful to those who perished and the families who carry their memories. God bless them and their loved ones.

— Jared Isaacman (@rookisaacman) November 2, 2026

What happens now?

NTSB officials stressed that it remains too early to identify a cause, with analysis of recorder data, weather information and wreckage evidence expected to continue in the weeks and months ahead.

]]> Learjet 60 crash: How thunderstorms affect aircraft at cruising altitude https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/learjet-60-crash-thunderstorm-risks-cruising-altitude/ Mon, 02 Nov 2026 16:57:42 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=55295 Thunderstorms can reach above cruising altitude, bringing turbulence and icing hazards. The Florida Learjet 60 crash highlights questions investigators must examine.

The post Learjet 60 crash: How thunderstorms affect aircraft at cruising altitude appeared first on AGN.

]]>
In Brief 4 min read
  • Thunderstorms can extend above cruising altitude, exposing aircraft to powerful air currents, turbulence and icing hazards.
  • Airframe icing, ice-crystal icing and Mach tuck are distinct phenomena; none has been established as the cause of the Learjet crash.
  • The crew reported icing, turbulence and overspeed, but investigators must determine how the emergency developed and whether weather contributed.

The crew of the Learjet 60 that crashed in Florida on 1 November reported icing, turbulence and increasing precipitation before the aircraft entered a steep descent, killing all nine people aboard.

The jet was flying from Austin, Texas, to North Eleuthera in the Bahamas. According to Flightradar24’s review of air traffic control recordings, the crew requested a climb from around 35,000 feet to 37,000 feet before reporting a rapid descent and an overspeed condition.

Weather analysis published by MyRadar places a developing thunderstorm near the aircraft’s flight path. Its analysis suggests the storm grew from approximately 33,000 feet to 48,300 feet between 12:36 p.m. and 12:56 p.m., a period spanning the accident.

We’ve reviewed radar and temperature data surrounding the crash of N722BD. This loop depicts the rapid vertical development of a convective cell, which lofted plentiful moisture. The aircraft entered this cell at 12:47-48 p.m., encountering severe icing and turbulence. https://t.co/7qzeOsLAYO

— MyRadar Weather (@MyRadarWX) November 2, 2026

Those measurements do not establish the storm’s precise height when the Learjet encountered it. They do, however, illustrate why cruising altitude does not necessarily put an aircraft above the weather.

How thunderstorms affect aircraft at cruising altitude

Thunderstorms develop vertically, with powerful rising air currents carrying moisture high into the atmosphere. Their tops can extend above the cruising altitudes of commercial airliners and business jets.

Within and around these clouds, aircraft can encounter turbulence, strong updrafts and downdrafts, hail and icing. Rapid changes in airflow can alter an aircraft’s airspeed, angle of attack and flight path, placing additional demands on its flight controls and crew.

In severe encounters, turbulence can cause substantial changes in attitude and altitude. Extreme turbulence can impose loads capable of damaging an aircraft. However, neither a nearby storm nor a subsequent dive establishes that structural damage occurred.

Weather radar also has limitations. It primarily detects precipitation rather than directly displaying every hazardous air movement. A weak return does not necessarily mean smooth or harmless conditions, particularly near the upper parts of a storm.

FAA guidance consequently emphasises avoiding thunderstorms, rather than using radar to find a route through them. Datalink weather imagery is intended for broader route planning, not close-range manoeuvring between rapidly changing storm cells.

Why icing can still threaten aircraft at altitude

Conventional airframe icing occurs when supercooled liquid droplets strike an aircraft and freeze. Clear ice forms when the water spreads before freezing, producing a relatively transparent deposit that can change the shape of an aerodynamic surface.

The resulting loss of performance is not simply about added weight. Ice can disrupt airflow, reduce lift, increase drag and cause a wing or tail surface to stall at a lower angle of attack than it would when clean.

At very low temperatures, however, the type of moisture matters. Below approximately −40°C, conventional supercooled-liquid-water icing becomes physically unlikely, and ice crystals become the more relevant concern.

Ice crystals generally do not accumulate on cold external surfaces in the same way as liquid droplets. But in high concentrations, they can partially melt and accumulate within warmer parts of turbine engines or affect heated sensors. They can also be difficult for conventional airborne weather radar to detect.

The Learjet crew’s icing report therefore warrants investigation, but it does not establish what accumulated, where it formed or whether it affected control.

What is Mach tuck, and how does it differ from icing?

Mach tuck is a high-speed aerodynamic effect, not a form of icing.

As an aircraft’s Mach number increases, airflow over parts of its wing can become supersonic even while the aircraft itself remains below the speed of sound. Shock waves develop, and changes in the pressure distribution can shift the wing’s effective lifting force rearwards, creating a nose-down pitching tendency.

Associated airflow separation can also produce buffet and affect handling. Aircraft are designed with operating limits and control systems to manage their high-speed characteristics, but exceeding those limits can make recovery more difficult.

The Learjet crew reported overspeed during the descent. That makes its speed history relevant, but overspeed alone does not establish that Mach tuck occurred, or whether excessive speed preceded or followed the initial loss of control.

NTSB investigation will examine the sequence

The National Transportation Safety Board is investigating and is expected to provide an update at a briefing in West Palm Beach on 2 November.

Investigators will need to establish how the aircraft’s flight path, weather exposure and any aerodynamic or mechanical problems developed together. The crew’s reports and available tracking data describe a rapidly escalating emergency; they do not yet explain its cause.

In Brief 4 min read

  • Demand remains resilient despite reduced capacity, helping carriers sustain strong fares in accessible markets.
  • Airbus remains confident in the Middle East’s long-term aviation growth, supported by its hub connectivity, but says airport infrastructure must expand.

Airlines around the world – and particularly in the Middle East – are adapting to airspace closures and disrupted operations by shifting capacity to alternative routes, with demand remaining strong enough to support high yields despite the loss of some capacity, according to Airbus vice-president for the region Grainne Van den Berg.

Speaking at Routes World 2026 in Frankfurt, Van den Berg said carriers were successfully navigating the disruption by demonstrating resilience and agility, moving aircraft to markets where operations remain viable rather than allowing capacity to sit idle.

Airlines are dealing with airspace closures and ‘destination volatility’

“As an industry, we’ve been facing airspace closures for quite a while with Russia and Ukraine, but now we have additional airspace closures in the Middle East, which are adding 45 – sometimes 90 – minutes to routes,” she said.

“Some routes are … not viable anymore, or they’re costing more, and you might not be getting the utilisation you had planned out of your aircraft.

“Not only are we dealing with airspace closures, we are also dealing with destination volatility. It is not just that we have to fly around zones, but sometimes those destinations are just not available anymore.”

Highlighting the industry’s “agility and ability to adapt”, Van den Berg added: “There is some structural capacity being taken out of the market. It is not really that the demand has disappeared, but that structurally the capacity is not being delivered to the market.”

Airlines shift capacity to alternative markets

Van den Berg said carriers were responding by redirecting aircraft towards markets that remain accessible, either by adding capacity or reallocating where aircraft are being deployed to match that demand, as well as deploying more fuel-efficient aircraft where possible.

“If we take, for example, Air France, [they] haven’t been flying to Dubai for several months now, but they’ve just redeployed that capacity directly onto Asian routes. For example, India, Japan and Thailand.”

She also highlighted the response of Kuwait-based Jazeera Airways, which moved its operation to an airport in north-eastern Saudi Arabia while Kuwait’s airport was closed for 57 days.

“Jazeera just upped its entire operation and moved it to an airport in the northeast of Saudi Arabia; that was quite some agility … to do that during that tough time.”

The airline maintained a limited flying schedule by bussing passengers across the border.

Riyadh Air is doing something similar. Since October 25, selected Riyadh Air flights have been operated via Al Qassim Airport after Riyadh’s primary airport was closed following Houthi airstrikes.

Another key strength for the airline sector is fleet flexibility, enabling carriers to match the right-sized aircraft to the routes they can continue to operate. 

Van den Berg said recently delivered aircraft had been welcomed by Middle Eastern carriers partly because their lower fuel consumption could help reduce operating costs.

Read more: Middle East conflict reshapes Australia travel patterns as air routes shift Read more: Middle East conflict reshapes Australia travel patterns as air routes shift

Demand remains despite reduced capacity

While the crisis has removed capacity from some markets, Van den Berg argued that this should not be seen as proof of a collapse in demand for air travel.

“There are still a lot of markets where there is an opportunity to defend yields,” she said.

Airlines are having to contend with higher fuel bills and longer flight times, but some routes can still attract strong fares. 

However, the outlook remains uncertain, with conflict and airspace closures likely to remain an ongoing headache for the industry.

Van den Berg said growth projections for the sector in 2026 had weakened as a result of the geopolitical volatility, with International Air Transport Association figures showing a contraction in traffic in August, although year-to-date numbers remained slightly positive.

Long-term Middle East growth outlook remains intact

Despite the short-term pressures, Van den Berg said the longer-term prognosis for the industry remained strong, with the Middle East well positioned to connect major population centres in Europe, Asia and Africa.

An eight-hour flight from the Gulf reaches about 80% of the world’s population, she said, and hubs in the region would continue to play an important role in connecting passengers travelling between cities that might not support direct services.

She said Airbus’ expectation was that the industry would continue expanding over the coming two decades, with Airbus forecasting demand for about 42,000 new aircraft across all manufacturers. 

Delivering that growth will also require additional airport capacity and investment in infrastructure, she added. 

“I know we’re having a tough time today, but you’ve seen the long-term trajectory. I think it’s going in the right direction. Be ready to capture that when it comes back.”

]]> Learjet 60 crash: What is a horizontal stabiliser, and why is it essential to flight? https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/learjet-60-crash-horizontal-stabiliser-explained/ Mon, 02 Nov 2026 12:15:19 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=55222 The horizontal stabiliser is crucial to the Learjet’s pitch stability. The post Learjet 60 crash: What is a horizontal stabiliser, and why is it essential to flight? appeared first on AGN.

]]>
In Brief 4 min read
  • The horizontal stabiliser provides pitch stability, while its elevators allow pilots to control the aircraft’s nose-up and nose-down movement.
  • Footage has prompted suggestions that the Learjet 60’s stabiliser was missing before impact, but this remains unconfirmed.
  • Even if it separated in flight, investigators must establish whether that triggered the loss of control or happened during the subsequent dive.

Following yesterday’s tragic crash of a Learjet 60 in Florida, attention is turning to a piece of the aircraft that appears to be missing in the harrowing crash footage.

The horizontal stabiliser is a small, wing-like surface that sits on the tail and keeps the aircraft in balance. On the Learjet 60, it sits at the top of the vertical tail fin, forming the crossbar of the aircraft’s distinctive T-tail.

For any conventionally configured aircraft, this piece of the tail is absolutely essential to safe and controlled flight. While the wings provide lift, the horizontal stabiliser is how pilots maintain and control the angle of the aircraft’s nose.

What we know about the Florida Learjet crash so far What we know about the Florida Learjet crash so far

How a horizontal stabiliser works

To understand the role of a horizontal stabiliser, it helps to think of an aircraft as a seesaw that pivots around its centre of gravity.

Forces acting on the wings, fuselage and engines can affect the aircraft’s pitch – the angle of its nose in relation to the horizon. Adding a horizontal stabiliser creates an additional aerodynamic force a long way to the rear of that pivot, balancing out these forces.

In normal flight conditions, the force generated by the horizontal stabiliser pushes the tail downwards, counterbalancing the nose-down tendencies of aircraft. It also helps control and alleviate unwanted changes in pitch caused by disturbances such as turbulence.

The tail assembly, also known as the rear empennage, has inbuilt control surfaces pilots can use to maintain safe progress of the flight. The vertical stabiliser features the rudder, which controls the side-to-side movement of the plane, or yaw. The horizontal stabiliser has elevators, which control the pitch up and down.

Most aircraft have a horizontal stabiliser, although they may look very different. Modern commercial planes like the Boeing 737 and Airbus A320 have a conventional stabiliser, located at the base of the vertical stabiliser. But older aircraft and some private jets have a T-tail stabiliser, positioned at the top of the vertical stabiliser.

Wherever it is located, this part of the aircraft is vital to controlled flight. If it becomes stuck, malfunctions or tears off, the consequences can be disastrous.

What happens when an aircraft loses its horizontal stabiliser?

A damaged or malfunctioning horizontal stabiliser can lead to anything from a manageable trim failure to an immediate and total loss of control. It all depends on what’s happened to that piece of tail and whether it can still produce a balancing force.

If the part suddenly disappears or becomes detached, the nose of the aircraft can pitch down sharply. With no elevators to use, the pilots may lose the pitch-control authority needed to recover.

An example of this was the tragic crash of a Dan Air Boeing 707 in 1977, where the right side horizontal stabiliser detached from the empennage on approach to the airport at Lusaka, Zambia. Eyewitnesses saw a large piece of the tail separate, and the aircraft immediately pitched nose down and impacted the ground, killing all six on board.

In some cases, the stabiliser doesn’t need to detach entirely for the results to be disastrous. In 2000, an MD-83 operating Alaska Airlines Flight 261 suffered a failure of the jackscrew that controlled the elevators in the horizontal stabiliser. The resulting loss of control caused an unrecoverable dive; the aircraft impacted the Pacific Ocean, and all 88 people on board lost their lives.

There have also been incidents involving issues with the horizontal stabiliser where trim has jammed or run away, or ice has affected its functionality.

What happened to the horizontal stabiliser in the Learjet 60 Florida crash?

Observers have noted that the footage from the Learjet crash appears to show the horizontal stabiliser missing. The aircraft had reported moderate turbulence prior to the dive, but that doesn’t necessarily mean the stabiliser separated in flight.

The reported turbulence and the pilot’s mention of icing to air traffic control could have resulted in a weather related upset that was unrelated to the missing stabiliser. What we do know is that the aircraft plummeted to the ground very fast, with Flightradar data suggesting speeds of more than 32,000 feet per minute at its peak. Such extreme speeds could have resulted in a separation of the horizontal stabiliser on descent.

Had the horizontal stabiliser failed, detached or otherwise malfunctioned in flight, a sudden nose down dive would be a likely outcome, but it doesn’t necessarily explain why this accident occured. Should this be the case, there is a chance investigators will find this part of the aircraft away from the crash site, somewhere along the flight path.

Of course, there is also the possibility that the low resolution dashcam footage of the crash just didn’t capture the horizontal stabiliser due to the speed of the crash. A thin surface such as this could be difficult to distiguish in such footage.

It is now the job of the air crash investigation team to establish the cause of the incident. The complete destruction of the wreckage on impact will make that job harder, but flight data recorders, cockpit voice recorders and other data will add valuable evidence to the outcome of this tragic event.

In Brief 7 min read
  • India’s new air force chief has prioritised Tejas Mk1A, LCA Mk2 and AMCA fighters to rebuild a fleet operating around 29 squadrons against an authorised 42.
  • Tejas Mk1A delivery delays remain the immediate challenge, while the Mk2 and AMCA are targeting first flights in 2027 and 2028 respectively.
  • The IAF needs 36–40 new fighters annually to restore combat strength, with additional Rafales and other foreign aircraft under consideration to bridge the gap.

India’s new Air Force chief has made restoring the service’s depleted fighter strength his top priority, placing the Tejas Mk1A, the larger LCA Mk2 and the country’s planned fifth-generation stealth fighter at the centre of his modernisation plans.

Air Chief Marshal Ashutosh Dixit, who took charge as the 29th Chief of the Air Staff on 1 November, said the Indian Air Force (IAF) would pursue indigenous aircraft, weapons and sensors while rebuilding its combat squadrons towards their authorised strength.

“The Tejas Mk-1A and Mk-2, AMCA (a fifth-generation stealth fighter jet), and Indian weapons and sensors are our highest priority,” Dixit said in his first public comments after assuming command.

“We will fight with Indian solutions, and we will hold them in numbers that meet our operational demands. Our responsibility is to fight and win, but most importantly it is to deter conflict through credible air power.”

His remarks come as the IAF faces one of its most difficult fleet renewal periods in decades. Ageing aircraft are being retired, replacements have been delayed and several of the fighters expected to form the backbone of the future fleet remain years away from operational service.

Dixit has inherited an air force operating around 29 fighter squadrons against an authorised strength of about 42. The shortage has become increasingly pressing as India seeks to maintain its combat capability along its borders with China and Pakistan.

“Every squadron, every radar, every air defence unit along with each and every air warrior must be ready to respond at a moment’s notice,” Dixit said. “Restoring our combat strength towards the sanctioned level will be my foremost task.”

Tejas Mk1A deliveries remain the immediate challenge

The most urgent requirement is getting the Tejas Mk1A into operational service in sufficient numbers.

Developed by Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL), the single-engine fighter is an improved version of the original Tejas, incorporating an active electronically scanned array radar, upgraded electronic warfare equipment and improved weapons capability.

India has ordered 180 Mk1A aircraft under two contracts. The aircraft are intended to replace ageing fighters and provide the IAF with a larger fleet of domestically manufactured combat jets.

Deliveries, however, have fallen behind schedule, partly because of interruptions in the supply of GE Aerospace F404-IN20 engines from the United States.

In February, HAL said five Mk1A fighters were ready for delivery after meeting key contractual requirements. Another nine aircraft had been built and flown but were awaiting engines.

The delays have exposed a problem that extends beyond aircraft manufacturing. Even when airframes are available, the IAF needs a reliable supply of engines, spare parts and maintenance facilities to keep them operational.

As Aerospace Global News reported in April, GE Aerospace and the IAF signed an agreement to establish an F404 engine repair and overhaul facility in India. The IAF will own and operate the depot, while GE will provide training, equipment and technical support.

The arrangement is intended to reduce the need to send engines overseas for major repairs and improve the availability of the Tejas fleet.

The Mk1A is therefore the programme most likely to influence the IAF’s squadron strength in the near term. The larger Mk2 and AMCA remain development projects.

LCA Mk2 targets first flight in 2027

India’s next step is the LCA Mk2, a substantially larger and more capable aircraft than the existing Tejas.

The medium-weight fighter is being developed by the Aeronautical Development Agency (ADA) and HAL to eventually replace aircraft such as the Jaguar, Mirage 2000 and MiG-29.

According to current planning, the oldest Jaguars are expected to begin retiring between 2028 and 2031, with the upgraded DARIN III aircraft likely to remain operational slightly longer.

To avoid a sudden drop in squadron strength, the IAF is now considering extending the service life of its Mirage 2000 fleet beyond its original retirement timeline.

“Initially expected to retire around 2035, the aircraft may now remain operational until 2038 or even 2039, providing a critical buffer as newer aircraft enter service,” an official at the Ministry of Defence had informed AGN recently.

Unlike the Mk1A, which uses the GE F404 engine, the Mk2 will be powered by the more powerful GE F414 engine. It is designed to carry heavier weapons loads, operate over longer distances and undertake a wider range of air combat and strike missions.

The aircraft is expected to incorporate an indigenous Uttam active electronically scanned array radar, an infrared search-and-track system and Indian-developed weapons. The programme has not yet reached its first flight.

Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh recently indicated that the Mk2 prototype is expected to fly between June and September 2027, reflecting a slippage of several months in the development schedule.

That timetable is important, but a successful first flight would mark the beginning of flight testing rather than the aircraft’s entry into service. The prototype would still have to undergo extensive trials before production aircraft could be delivered to operational squadrons.

The IAF is therefore unlikely to receive meaningful numbers of Mk2 fighters in time to resolve its immediate squadron shortage.

India’s stealth fighter aims for 2028 first flight

The Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA) is the most ambitious of India’s three indigenous fighter programmes.

Designed as a twin-engine, fifth-generation aircraft, the AMCA is intended to combine stealth characteristics with advanced sensors, electronic warfare systems and the ability to carry weapons internally.

Internal weapon bays are particularly important because weapons carried beneath an aircraft increase its radar signature. The AMCA will also have external hardpoints for missions where carrying a larger weapons load takes priority over remaining difficult to detect.

The initial version is planned to use GE F414 engines, while a later variant is expected to incorporate a more powerful engine developed in India.

Defence Secretary Singh has indicated that the first AMCA prototype is scheduled to fly in September 2028.The programme is still at the stage of selecting an industrial partner to build its prototypes.

As AGN reported in September, three private-sector teams were competing for the development and production contract after the bid deadline was extended to 30 October.

Tata Advanced Systems is competing independently, while Larsen & Toubro has partnered with Bharat Electronics and Dynamatic Technologies. A third consortium comprises Bharat Forge, BEML and Data Patterns.

The selected company will work with ADA to build five flying prototypes and a structural test article. The programme envisages an extensive flight-test campaign before the aircraft can enter production.

The timetable leaves a substantial gap between the IAF’s immediate requirement for more fighters and the arrival of an operational Indian stealth aircraft.

Read about the AMCA race as 7 firms bid to build India’s 5th-generation stealth fighter Read about the AMCA race as 7 firms bid to build India’s 5th-generation stealth fighter

Falling squadron numbers increase pressure on procurement

The scale of that gap was highlighted by Dixit’s predecessor, Air Chief Marshal A.P. Singh, shortly before his retirement.

As AGN reported in October, Singh said the IAF needed to induct between 36 and 40 fighters annually over the next few years to rebuild its combat strength.

“We need to induct two fighter squadrons every year. That means anything between 36 and 40 aircraft should be produced and inducted,” he said.

He also acknowledged that India might have to consider additional foreign fighters if its indigenous programmes slipped further.

“We may have to look at other fighter platforms in case of delays in AMCA fifth-gen and other programmes to fill in the gaps,” Singh told reporters.

Russia has offered India the Su-57 fifth-generation fighter, although Singh said no decision had been taken.

India is also pursuing the acquisition of 114 additional Dassault Rafale fighters under its Multi-Role Fighter Aircraft programme.

The proposed purchase is intended to help address the squadron shortage while domestic fighter production expands. Negotiations have yet to produce a final contract.

AGN previously reported that access to sensitive Rafale software had emerged as a point of disagreement between India and France. The issue concerns India’s ability to integrate indigenous weapons and modify certain aircraft systems without depending entirely on the manufacturer.

The IAF’s challenge is therefore not simply choosing between Indian and foreign fighters. It must obtain enough aircraft quickly while building a domestic industry capable of producing, maintaining and upgrading them over several decades.

New chief outlines VAYU modernisation plan

Dixit has set out his priorities under a framework called VAYU ( also means AIR in Hindi language), covering vigilance and readiness, self-reliance, innovation and unity of effort.

The plan includes greater use of artificial intelligence in command-and-control systems, stronger counter-drone defences, improved maintenance and closer operational coordination with the Army and Navy.

“U stands for unity of effort,” Dixit said. “In step with the vision of JAI — Jointness, Aatmanirbharta and Innovation — we will plan and fight as one alongside our Army, our Navy and our national agencies.”

An experimental test pilot and qualified flying instructor with more than 3,500 flying hours, Dixit has served as Vice Chief of the Air Staff, commander of Central Air Command and Chief of Integrated Defence Staff to the Chairman Chiefs of Staff Committee.

His immediate test will be the pace at which new fighters reach operational squadrons.

 ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ */
/* ── Root variables ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
:root {
 --sie-hdr-brand:       #0056b3;        /* SIE brand blue                      */
 --sie-hdr-brand-light: #1a6fc4;
 --sie-hdr-bar-h:       64px;           /* nav bar height — fixed, prevents CLS */

 position: relative;
 z-index: 1000;
}
/* ── Navigation bar ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__bar {
 height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 background: var(--sie-hdr-bar-bg);

 border-bottom: 1px solid var(--sie-hdr-bar-border);
}
.sie-hdr__inner {
 max-width: 1280px;
 height: 100%;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 24px;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 32px;
}
/* ── Logo ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__logo {

 text-decoration: none;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
}
.sie-hdr__logo-img {
 height: 54px;
 width: auto;
 display: block;
}
.sie-hdr__logo-text {
 font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif;
 font-size: 17px;
 font-weight: 700;
 color: #fff;
 letter-spacing: -0.01em;
 white-space: nowrap;
}

.sie-hdr__nav {

 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list {
 list-style: none;
 margin: 0;
 padding: 0;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list li {
 position: relative;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list a,
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;

 font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif;
 font-size: 14px;
 font-weight: 500;
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 text-decoration: none;
 border-radius: 8px;
 transition: background 0.15s ease, color 0.15s ease;
 white-space: nowrap;
 min-height: 48px; /* WCAG touch target */
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 background: none;
 border: none;
 cursor: pointer;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list a:hover,
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle:hover,

 margin: 0;

.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(2) {

}
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(3) {
 transform: translateY(-7px) rotate(-45deg);
}

 user-ui.php's desktop bar uses position:absolute; top:20px; right:30px — that

 Fixed-position children (auth drawer, mobile bar, destinations panel) are

 three on .sie-hdr__bar).
 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 position: static !important;
 top: auto !important;
 right: auto !important;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 margin-left: auto;

 user-ui's default .se-ai-icon is 86×86 px (fine for the mobile bottom bar),

.sie-hdr .se-shortlist-link,

}

.sie-hdr .se-fav-desktop-link:hover {

#sie-auth-drawer { position:fixed; inset:0; z-index:2147482000; background:rgba(12,113,195,.42); opacity:0; visibility:hidden; pointer-events:auto; transition:opacity .25s ease; backdrop-filter:saturate(1.05) blur(1px); }
#sie-auth-drawer.open { opacity:1; visibility:visible; }
#sie-auth-drawer .sie-auth-inner { position:absolute; top:0; right:0; height:100%; width:min(560px,100%); background:linear-gradient(180deg,#ffffff 0%,#f7fbff 100%); box-shadow:-12px 0 24px rgba(0,0,0,.16); padding:26px 24px 28px; overflow:auto; will-change:transform,opacity; transform:translateX(28px); opacity:0; transition:transform .38s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1),opacity .38s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1); z-index:2147482100; }
#sie-auth-drawer.open .sie-auth-inner { transform:translateX(0); opacity:1; }
@media (max-width:768px){
 #sie-auth-drawer .sie-auth-inner { top:auto; bottom:0; right:auto; left:0; width:100%; height:85vh; border-top-left-radius:16px; border-top-right-radius:16px; box-shadow:0 -12px 24px rgba(0,0,0,.16); transform:translateY(28px); }
 #sie-auth-drawer.open .sie-auth-inner { transform:translateY(0); }
}
.sie-auth-close { background:transparent; border:0; font-size:30px; line-height:1; cursor:pointer; position:absolute; right:14px; top:10px; color:#0b3770; opacity:.9; }
.sie-auth-close:hover { opacity:1; }
.sie-auth-title { margin:0 0 6px; font-size:1.6rem; font-weight:800; color:#0b3770; }
.sie-auth-intro { margin:0 0 16px; color:#163b6b; font-size:1.02rem; line-height:1.45; }
.sie-hero { display:flex; align-items:center; justify-content:space-between; background:#eef5ff; border:1px solid #dbe8ff; border-radius:14px; padding:10px 12px; margin:10px 0 14px; }
.sie-hero-left { display:flex; align-items:center; gap:12px; }
.sie-hero-avatar { width:44px; height:auto; border-radius:50%; }
.sie-hero-copy { display:flex; gap:10px; flex-wrap:wrap; font-size:.92rem; color:#0b3770; }
.sie-hero-line { display:flex; align-items:center; gap:6px; }
.sie-hero-line i { font-size:.95rem; color:#1e66f5; }
.sie-toggle { --pad:4px; position:relative; display:grid; grid-template-columns:1fr 1fr; background:#e9f2ff; border-radius:999px; padding:var(--pad); margin-bottom:12px; width:fit-content; min-width:320px; }
.sie-toggle-btn { position:relative; z-index:1; border:0; background:transparent; padding:10px 18px; border-radius:999px; font-weight:800; color:#0b3770; cursor:pointer; display:flex; align-items:center; gap:10px; line-height:1; }
.sie-toggle-btn.active { color:#fff; }
.sie-toggle-pill { position:absolute; top:var(--pad); left:var(--pad); width:calc(50% - var(--pad)); height:calc(100% - var(--pad)*2); border-radius:999px; background:#1e66f5; box-shadow:0 4px 10px rgba(12,113,195,.28); transition:transform .25s ease; will-change:transform; }
.sie-auth-panel label { font-weight:600; margin-top:12px; display:block; color:#003B73; }
.sie-label-strong { font-weight:800; color:#0f172a; font-size:1.05rem; }
.sie-auth-panel .input { width:100%; padding:12px 14px; border:1px solid #d4dceb; border-radius:12px; background:#fff; transition:box-shadow .15s ease,border-color .15s ease; }
.sie-auth-panel .input:focus { outline:none; border-color:#1e66f5; box-shadow:0 0 0 3px rgba(30,102,245,.14); }
.sie-auth-btn { display:inline-flex; align-items:center; gap:8px; border:0; padding:12px 18px; border-radius:999px; cursor:pointer; background:#1e66f5; color:#fff; font-weight:800; box-shadow:0 6px 18px rgba(30,102,245,.18); transition:transform .05s ease,box-shadow .2s ease; }
.sie-auth-btn:hover { box-shadow:0 10px 24px rgba(30,102,245,.22); }
.sie-auth-btn:active { transform:translateY(1px); }
.sie-consent { margin:10px 0 4px; }
.sie-consent-label { font-size:.95rem; color:#0b3770; }
.sie-consent input[type="checkbox"] { margin-right:8px; vertical-align:text-bottom; }
.sie-consent a { color:#1e66f5; text-decoration:underline; }
.forgot-password-link { margin:10px 0 0; }
.forgot-password-link a { color:#1e66f5; text-decoration:underline; }
#sie-auth-reset-form .input, #sie-auth-reset-form input[type="text"] { width:100%; padding:12px 14px; border:1px solid #d4dceb; border-radius:12px; background:#fff; margin-bottom:20px; }
#sie-auth-reset-form .input:focus, #sie-auth-reset-form input[type="text"]:focus { outline:none; border-color:#1e66f5; box-shadow:0 0 0 3px rgba(30,102,245,.14); }
.status-message { text-align:center; color:#1e66f5; font-weight:700; padding:12px; background:#eef5ff; border-left:4px solid #1e66f5; border-radius:8px; margin:10px 0; }
.password-reset-error { text-align:center; background:#ffeaea; color:#8b1d1d; border-left:4px solid #dc3545; border-radius:8px; padding:12px; margin-top:10px; }
.password-reset-success { text-align:center; background:#eaf9ef; color:#14532d; border-left:4px solid #22c55e; border-radius:8px; padding:12px; margin-top:10px; }
body.sie-auth-open .grecaptcha-badge { visibility:visible !important; opacity:1 !important; z-index:2147483647 !important; }
.sie-auth-illustration { display:flex; justify-content:center; align-items:flex-end; margin:18px 0 6px; position:relative; padding-bottom:4px; }
.sie-auth-illustration::before { content:""; position:absolute; bottom:0; left:50%; transform:translateX(-50%); width:min(78%,420px); height:26px; border-radius:999px; background:radial-gradient(closest-side,rgba(30,102,245,.18),rgba(30,102,245,0)); filter:blur(6px); pointer-events:none; }
.sie-auth-illustration .hero-image { width:min(92%,420px); height:auto; display:block; filter:drop-shadow(0 14px 26px rgba(30,102,245,.16)); }
@media (max-width:420px){ .sie-auth-illustration .hero-image { width:92%; } }
/* ==================== DESTINATIONS PANEL ==================== */

.sie-dest-panel { position:fixed; inset:0; z-index:2147483000; display:flex; align-items:stretch; justify-content:flex-end; opacity:0; visibility:hidden; pointer-events:none; transition:opacity .25s ease,visibility .25s; }
.sie-dest-panel.open { opacity:1; visibility:visible; pointer-events:auto; }

.sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet { transform:translateX(0); opacity:1; }
@media (max-width:767px){

}
.sie-dest-panel__header { display:flex; align-items:center; justify-content:space-between; margin-bottom:6px; flex-shrink:0; }
.sie-dest-panel__titlewrap { display:flex; align-items:center; gap:10px; }
.sie-dest-panel__globe { font-size:22px; color:#1e66f5; line-height:1; }
.sie-dest-panel__title { font-size:1.5rem; font-weight:800; color:#0b3770; margin:0; line-height:1.2; }
.sie-dest-panel__close { background:transparent; border:0; font-size:22px; color:#0b3770; cursor:pointer; padding:6px 8px; border-radius:8px; line-height:1; opacity:.75; transition:opacity .15s,background .15s; flex-shrink:0; }
.sie-dest-panel__close:hover { opacity:1; background:#f0f4ff; }
.sie-dest-panel__sub { color:#466087; font-size:.94rem; margin:0 0 20px; flex-shrink:0; }
.sie-dest-panel__grid { display:grid; grid-template-columns:repeat(4,1fr); gap:14px; flex:1; align-content:start; }
@media (max-width:620px){ .sie-dest-panel__grid { grid-template-columns:repeat(2,1fr); gap:10px; } }
@media (min-width:621px) and (max-width:860px){ .sie-dest-panel__grid { grid-template-columns:repeat(3,1fr); } }
.sie-dest-panel__card { position:relative; display:block; aspect-ratio:3/2; border-radius:12px; overflow:hidden; text-decoration:none; background:#1d3557; }

 DESTINATIONS PANEL  — overlay + grid
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
 /* Outer layer: covers full viewport */
 .sie-dest-panel {
 position: fixed;
 inset: 0;
 z-index: 2147483000;
 display: flex;
 align-items: stretch;
 justify-content: flex-end;
 opacity: 0;
 visibility: hidden;
 pointer-events: none;
 transition: opacity .25s ease, visibility .25s;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open {
 opacity: 1;
 visibility: visible;
 pointer-events: auto;
 }
 /* Backdrop */
 .sie-dest-panel__backdrop {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 background: rgba(11, 55, 112, .52);
 backdrop-filter: blur(3px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(3px);
 cursor: pointer;
 }
 /* Sheet — right-panel on desktop */
 .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 position: relative;
 z-index: 1;
 width: min(800px, 100%);
 height: 100%;
 background: #fff;
 overflow-y: auto;
 -webkit-overflow-scrolling: touch;
 padding: 26px 26px 40px;
 display: flex;
 flex-direction: column;
 gap: 0;
 transform: translateX(28px);
 opacity: 0;
 transition: transform .38s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1), opacity .38s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1);
 box-shadow: -20px 0 48px rgba(0,0,0,.18);
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 transform: translateX(0);
 opacity: 1;
 }
 /* Mobile: bottom-sheet */
 @media (max-width: 767px) {
 .sie-dest-panel {
 align-items: flex-end;
 justify-content: stretch;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 width: 100%;
 height: 92vh;
 border-top-left-radius: 22px;
 border-top-right-radius: 22px;
 padding: 20px 16px 40px;
 transform: translateY(28px);
 box-shadow: 0 -16px 48px rgba(0,0,0,.18);
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 transform: translateY(0);
 }
 }
 /* ── Header ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__header {
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 justify-content: space-between;
 margin-bottom: 6px;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__titlewrap {
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 10px;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__globe {
 font-size: 22px;
 color: #1e66f5;
 line-height: 1;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__title {
 font-size: 1.5rem;
 font-weight: 800;
 color: #0b3770;
 margin: 0;
 line-height: 1.2;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__close {
 background: transparent;
 border: 0;
 font-size: 22px;
 color: #0b3770;
 cursor: pointer;
 padding: 6px 8px;
 border-radius: 8px;
 line-height: 1;
 opacity: .75;
 transition: opacity .15s, background .15s;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__close:hover {
 opacity: 1;
 background: #f0f4ff;
 }
 /* Subheading */
 .sie-dest-panel__sub {
 color: #466087;
 font-size: .94rem;
 margin: 0 0 20px;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 /* ── Country grid ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 display: grid;
 grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr);
 gap: 14px;
 /* allow this to grow and scroll */
 flex: 1;
 align-content: start;
 }
 @media (max-width: 620px) {
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr);
 gap: 10px;
 }
 }
 @media (min-width: 621px) and (max-width: 860px) {
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
 }
 }
 /* ── Country card ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__card {
 position: relative;
 display: block;
 aspect-ratio: 3 / 2;
 border-radius: 12px;
 overflow: hidden;
 text-decoration: none;
 background: #1d3557;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card--no-img .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 background: linear-gradient(135deg, #1d3557 0%, #1e66f5 100%);
 }
 /* Hero image layer — scales on hover */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 transition: transform .4s ease;
 will-change: transform;
 }
 /* <img> fills the card exactly like background-size:cover did.
 loading="lazy" means the browser only fetches each image when the
 panel opens and the card enters the viewport — saving ~30 MB of
 upfront image requests on every page that includes this panel. */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-img {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 width: 100%;
 height: 100%;
 object-fit: cover;
 object-position: center;
 display: block;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card:hover .sie-dest-panel__card-bg,
 .sie-dest-panel__card:focus-visible .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 transform: scale(1.07);
 }
 /* Gradient overlay + text */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-body {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 display: flex;
 flex-direction: column;
 justify-content: flex-end;
 padding: 10px 12px 10px;
 background: linear-gradient(
 to top,
 rgba(0, 0, 0, .72) 0%,
 rgba(0, 0, 0, .30) 55%,
 transparent 100%
 );
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card-name {
 color: #fff;
 font-weight: 700;
 font-size: .92rem;
 line-height: 1.2;
 text-shadow: 0 1px 5px rgba(0,0,0,.55);
 display: block;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow {
 display: block;
 color: rgba(255,255,255,0);
 font-size: .75rem;
 margin-top: 2px;
 transition: color .2s ease, transform .2s ease;
 line-height: 1;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card:hover .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow,
 .sie-dest-panel__card:focus-visible .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow {
 color: rgba(255,255,255,.9);
 transform: translateX(4px);
 }
 /* ── Body-scroll lock ── */
 body.sie-dest-panel-open {
 overflow: hidden;
 }
 /* ── Country interest heart ── */
 .sie-country-heart {
 position: absolute;
 top: 8px;
 right: 8px;
 z-index: 10;
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 border: none;
 border-radius: 20px;
 padding: 4px 8px 4px 7px;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
 cursor: pointer;
 font-size: 13px;
 color: #94a3b8;
 box-shadow: 0 2px 8px rgba(0,0,0,.22);
 backdrop-filter: blur(6px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(6px);
 transition: color .18s, transform .18s, background .18s;
 line-height: 1;
 min-width: 28px;
 justify-content: center;
 }
 .sie-country-heart:hover {
 transform: scale(1.12);
 background: #fff;
 color: #ef4444;
 }
 .sie-country-heart.voted {
 color: #ef4444;
 background: #fff;
 }
 .sie-country-heart.voted i {
 animation: sie-heart-pop .35s cubic-bezier(.36,.07,.19,.97);
 }
 @keyframes sie-heart-pop {
 0%   { transform: scale(1); }
 40%  { transform: scale(1.45); }
 70%  { transform: scale(.88); }
 100% { transform: scale(1); }
 }
 .sie-country-heart__count {
 font-size: 11px;
 font-weight: 700;
 color: inherit;
 display: none;
 }
 .sie-country-heart.has-votes .sie-country-heart__count {
 display: inline;
 }
 /* ── Trigger button styles (for use in any menu) ── */
 /* Desktop globe icon */
 .se-dest-desktop-btn {
 font-size: 24px;
 color: #fff;
 text-decoration: none;
 cursor: pointer;
 transition: transform .2s, color .2s;
 position: relative;
 line-height: 1;
 background: transparent;
 border: 0;
 padding: 0;
 }
 .se-dest-desktop-btn:hover {
 transform: scale(1.15);
 color: #FFCC00;
 }
 /* Tooltip on desktop */
 @media (min-width: 1024px) {
 .se-dest-desktop-btn::after {
 content: "Study Destinations";
 position: absolute;
 bottom: -30px;
 left: 50%;
 transform: translateX(-50%);
 background: #007BFF;
 color: #fff;
 padding: 4px 8px;
 font-size: 12px;
 border-radius: 5px;
 opacity: 0;
 pointer-events: none;
 transition: opacity .2s;
 white-space: nowrap;
 }
 .se-dest-desktop-btn:hover::after {
 opacity: 1;
 }
 }
 /* Mobile pill button */
 .se-dest-btn {
 background: #0b3770 !important;
 color: #fff !important;
 }
 .se-dest-btn:hover {
 background: #1e66f5 !important;

<div class="ecl"><h2><strong>What is the Conference?</strong></h2>

<p>The <strong>Conference on the Future of Europe </strong>is the first transnational discussion with Europeans on how to address Europe’s challenges together. This is an opportunity to think about what citizens and&nbsp; civil society want for the European Union.</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

  <div class="eac-body lc-stripe-wrapper-text"><h2><strong>How does the Conference work?</strong></h2>

<p>Europeans can share ideas via the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Multilingual Digital Platform</a>, and both national and&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/assemblies/citizens-panels" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">European Citizens' Panels</a>. These contributions feed into the&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/plenary" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference Plenaries</a>.</p>

<p>The Conference&nbsp;offers a new public forum for an open, inclusive, and transparent debate with citizens around a number of key priorities and challenges.</p>

<h2><strong>How can you participate?</strong></h2>

<ul>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]--><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/processes?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">share your own ideas or support others’ ideas</a> on the multilingual digital Conference platform</li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->organise your own events and promote it by adding them to the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference platform</a></li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->take a look at the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/meetings" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">events organised by people across the EU</a></li>
</ul>

<h2><strong>What will the outcome be?</strong></h2>

<p>All of the ideas gathered and reports on events are published on the platform openly and transparently. These reports will then directly influence the discussions in the European Citizens’ Panels as well as in the Plenaries, where citizens will enter into a dialogue with national and European decision makers.</p>

<p>By spring 2022, the Conference will provide guidance on the future of Europe to the European institutions</p>

<p><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/getinvolved" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Get involved and make your voice heard when it comes to education, culture, youth, sport, and more</a>.</p>
